text: AI Model Access is a tactic used by adversaries to obtain some level of access to an AI model. This access serves as a foundation for gaining information, developing attacks, and providing input data to the model. The degree of access varies widely, ranging from complete knowledge of the model's internal architecture to physical access to the environment where the model's training data is collected. Adversaries may utilize different levels of access at various stages of an operation, from initial staging to the final impact on the target system. Access can be achieved directly through the system housing the model, via a publicly available API, or indirectly by interacting with a product or service that integrates AI into its processes.
name: AI Model Access
description:
The adversary is attempting to gain some level of access to an AI model.

AI Model Access enables techniques that use various types of access to the AI model that can be used by the adversary to gain information, develop attacks, and as a means to input data to the model.
The level of access can range from the full knowledge of the internals of the model to access to the physical environment where data is collected for use in the AI model.
The adversary may use varying levels of model access during the course of their attack, from staging the attack to impacting the target system.

Access to an AI model may require access to the system housing the model, the model may be publicly accessible via an API, or it may be accessed indirectly via interaction with a product or service that utilizes AI as part of its processes.

text: AI Attack Staging is a tactic that involves adversaries leveraging their knowledge of and access to a target system to tailor and prepare a specific attack against an AI model. This stage consists of various preparatory techniques, such as training proxy models, poisoning the target model, or crafting adversarial data to be fed into the system. Because some of these activities can be performed offline, they are often difficult to detect or mitigate. These techniques serve as a critical foundation for the adversary to successfully achieve their ultimate end goal.
name: AI Attack Staging
description:
The adversary is leveraging their knowledge of and access to the target system to tailor the attack.

AI Attack Staging consists of techniques adversaries use to prepare their attack on the target AI model.
Techniques can include training proxy models, poisoning the target model, and crafting adversarial data to feed the target model.
Some of these techniques can be performed in an offline manner and are thus difficult to mitigate.
These techniques are often used to achieve the adversary's end goal.

text: Reconnaissance is a tactic used by adversaries to gather information about an AI system to plan and support future operations. This process involves both active and passive techniques to collect data that aids in targeting, such as identifying a victim organization's AI capabilities and research efforts. The information gathered during reconnaissance is leveraged across other phases of the adversary lifecycle, allowing attackers to obtain relevant AI artifacts, target specific AI capabilities, tailor attacks to the particular models in use, or drive further reconnaissance efforts.
name: Reconnaissance
description:
The adversary is trying to gather information about the AI system they can use to plan future operations.

Reconnaissance consists of techniques that involve adversaries actively or passively gathering information that can be used to support targeting.
Such information may include details of the victim organizations' AI capabilities and research efforts.
This information can be leveraged by the adversary to aid in other phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as using gathered information to obtain relevant AI artifacts, targeting AI capabilities used by the victim, tailoring attacks to the particular models used by the victim, or to drive and lead further Reconnaissance efforts.

text: Resource Development is a tactic used by adversaries to establish the necessary resources required to support their operations. This process involves creating, purchasing, compromising, or stealing various assets that can be used for targeting, including infrastructure, accounts, capabilities, and AI artifacts. These developed resources are leveraged to facilitate other phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as AI attack staging.
name: Resource Development
description:
The adversary is trying to establish resources they can use to support operations.

Resource Development consists of techniques that involve adversaries creating,
purchasing, or compromising/stealing resources that can be used to support targeting.
Such resources include AI artifacts, infrastructure, accounts, or capabilities.
These resources can be leveraged by the adversary to aid in other phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as [AI Attack Staging](/tactics/AML.TA0001).

text: Initial Access is a tactic used by an adversary to gain an initial foothold within an AI system. This process involves employing various entry vectors to penetrate the target, which may be a network, a mobile device, or an edge device such as a sensor platform. The target system's AI capabilities may be hosted locally on the device or enabled through the cloud. The primary purpose of this tactic is to establish the first point of entry required to conduct further operations within the system.
name: Initial Access
description:
The adversary is trying to gain access to the AI system.

The target system could be a network, mobile device, or an edge device such as a sensor platform.
The AI capabilities used by the system could be local with onboard or cloud-enabled AI capabilities.

Initial Access consists of techniques that use various entry vectors to gain their initial foothold within the system.

text: Execution is a tactic that involves an adversary attempting to run malicious code embedded within software or AI artifacts. This tactic encompasses various techniques that result in adversary-controlled code being executed on either a local or remote system. Execution is often used in conjunction with other tactics to achieve broader objectives, such as stealing sensitive data or exploring a network. For instance, an adversary might utilize a remote access tool to execute a PowerShell script for the purpose of discovering other systems on a network.
name: Execution
description:
The adversary is trying to run malicious code embedded in AI artifacts or software.

Execution consists of techniques that result in adversary-controlled code running on a local or remote system.
Techniques that run malicious code are often paired with techniques from all other tactics to achieve broader goals, like exploring a network or stealing data.
For example, an adversary might use a remote access tool to run a PowerShell script that does [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018/).

text: Persistence is a tactic that adversaries use to maintain a consistent foothold within a system via AI artifacts or software. This tactic consists of various techniques designed to ensure continued access to systems even after restarts, credential changes, or other interruptions that would typically terminate a connection. In the context of AI, persistence often involves the use of modified machine learning artifacts, such as the introduction of poisoned training data or the deployment of manipulated AI models, to ensure the adversary's influence remains embedded in the environment.
name: Persistence
description:
The adversary is trying to maintain their foothold via AI artifacts or software.

Persistence consists of techniques that adversaries use to keep access to systems across restarts, changed credentials, and other interruptions that could cut off their access.
Techniques used for persistence often involve leaving behind modified ML artifacts such as poisoned training data or manipulated AI models.

text: Defense Evasion is a tactic used by adversaries to avoid detection throughout the course of a compromise. Its primary purpose is to bypass security measures and remain undetected while operating within a target environment. This includes the use of various techniques specifically designed to evade AI-enabled security software, such as malware detectors, ensuring the adversary can maintain their presence and achieve their objectives without triggering alerts.
name: Defense Evasion
description:
The adversary is trying to avoid being detected by AI-enabled security software.

Defense Evasion consists of techniques that adversaries use to avoid detection throughout their compromise.
Techniques used for defense evasion include evading AI-enabled security software such as malware detectors.

text: Discovery is a tactic used by adversaries to gain knowledge about an AI environment, system, and internal network. This process allows attackers to observe their surroundings and orient themselves before deciding on their next course of action. By exploring the area around their entry point, adversaries can determine what they control and identify resources that can be leveraged to achieve their current objectives. To accomplish this post-compromise information-gathering goal, adversaries frequently utilize native operating system tools.
name: Discovery
description:
The adversary is trying to figure out your AI environment.

Discovery consists of techniques an adversary may use to gain knowledge about the system and internal network.
These techniques help adversaries observe the environment and orient themselves before deciding how to act.
They also allow adversaries to explore what they can control and what's around their entry point in order to discover how it could benefit their current objective.
Native operating system tools are often used toward this post-compromise information-gathering objective.

text: Collection is a tactic used by adversaries to gather AI artifacts and other related information necessary to achieve their objectives. This process involves employing various techniques to identify and collect data from sources relevant to the adversary's goals. Once the information is gathered, it is frequently used to stage future operations or is targeted for exfiltration. Common sources for this type of collection include object stores, model repositories, container registries, and software repositories.
name: Collection
description:
The adversary is trying to gather AI artifacts and other related information relevant to their goal.

Collection consists of techniques adversaries may use to gather information and the sources information is collected from that are relevant to following through on the adversary's objectives.
Frequently, the next goal after collecting data is to steal (exfiltrate) the AI artifacts, or use the collected information to stage future operations.
Common target sources include software repositories, container registries, model repositories, and object stores.

text: Exfiltration is a tactic used by adversaries to steal AI artifacts or other sensitive information regarding an AI system. This process involves various techniques designed to remove data from a target network, often to acquire valuable intellectual property or to gather intelligence for staging future operations. To move data out of the network, adversaries typically transfer it through their established command and control channels or via alternate communication channels, sometimes implementing size limits on transmissions to avoid detection.
name: Exfiltration
description:
The adversary is trying to steal AI artifacts or other information about the AI system.

Exfiltration consists of techniques that adversaries may use to steal data from your network.
Data may be stolen for its valuable intellectual property, or for use in staging future operations.

Techniques for getting data out of a target network typically include transferring it over their command and control channel or an alternate channel and may also include putting size limits on the transmission.

text: Impact is a tactic used by adversaries to manipulate, interrupt, erode confidence in, or destroy AI systems and data. This tactic involves various techniques designed to disrupt availability or compromise integrity by manipulating operational and business processes. Adversaries may achieve this by destroying or tampering with data, or by subtly altering business processes to align with their goals while maintaining a facade of normal operation. These techniques are often employed to fulfill a final objective or to provide cover for a breach of confidentiality.
name: Impact
description:
The adversary is trying to manipulate, interrupt, erode confidence in, or destroy your AI systems and data.

Impact consists of techniques that adversaries use to disrupt availability or compromise integrity by manipulating business and operational processes.
Techniques used for impact can include destroying or tampering with data.
In some cases, business processes can look fine, but may have been altered to benefit the adversaries' goals.
These techniques might be used by adversaries to follow through on their end goal or to provide cover for a confidentiality breach.

text: Privilege Escalation is a tactic that adversaries use to gain higher-level permissions on a system or network. While an attacker may initially enter and explore a network with unprivileged access, they often require elevated permissions to successfully achieve their objectives. This is typically accomplished by exploiting system weaknesses, misconfigurations, and vulnerabilities. Examples of elevated access include obtaining SYSTEM or root level privileges, becoming a local administrator, or gaining access to user accounts with administrative capabilities or specific system functions. These techniques frequently overlap with persistence methods, as certain operating system features that allow an adversary to maintain access can also execute within an elevated context.
name: Privilege Escalation
description:
The adversary is trying to gain higher-level permissions.

Privilege Escalation consists of techniques that adversaries use to gain higher-level permissions on a system or network. Adversaries can often enter and explore a network with unprivileged access but require elevated permissions to follow through on their objectives. Common approaches are to take advantage of system weaknesses, misconfigurations, and vulnerabilities. Examples of elevated access include:
- SYSTEM/root level
- local administrator
- user account with admin-like access
- user accounts with access to specific system or perform specific function

These techniques often overlap with Persistence techniques, as OS features that let an adversary persist can execute in an elevated context.

text: Credential Access is a tactic used by adversaries to steal account names and passwords. This process involves various techniques, such as keylogging or credential dumping, to obtain sensitive authentication data. By acquiring legitimate credentials, adversaries can gain unauthorized access to systems, blend in with normal user activity to avoid detection, and create additional accounts to further their objectives within a network.
name: Credential Access
description:
The adversary is trying to steal account names and passwords.

Credential Access consists of techniques for stealing credentials like account names and passwords. Techniques used to get credentials include keylogging or credential dumping. Using legitimate credentials can give adversaries access to systems, make them harder to detect, and provide the opportunity to create more accounts to help achieve their goals.

text: Command and Control is a tactic used by adversaries to communicate with and manage compromised AI systems within a victim's network. This process involves employing various techniques to establish a communication channel, allowing the attacker to send instructions and maintain control over the affected systems. To avoid detection by security monitoring, adversaries often attempt to mimic normal, expected network traffic. The specific methods used to establish this control vary in their level of stealth, depending on the structure of the victim's network and the defenses in place.
name: Command and Control
description:
The adversary is trying to communicate with compromised AI systems to control them.

Command and Control consists of techniques that adversaries may use to communicate with systems under their control within a victim network. Adversaries commonly attempt to mimic normal, expected traffic to avoid detection. There are many ways an adversary can establish command and control with various levels of stealth depending on the victim's network structure and defenses.

text: Lateral Movement is a tactic used by adversaries to move through an AI environment to gain access to and control over other systems or components. By pivoting through the environment, attackers target AI Ops infrastructure, including model registries, experiment trackers, vector databases, notebooks, and training pipelines. This process allows adversaries to discover and exploit additional AI-related tools, services, and applications. AI agents are particularly valuable targets during lateral movement because they often possess higher permission levels than standard user accounts.
name: Lateral Movement
description:
The adversary is trying to move through your AI environment.

Lateral Movement consists of techniques that adversaries may use to gain access to and control other systems or components in the environment. Adversaries may pivot towards AI Ops infrastructure such as model registries, experiment trackers, vector databases, notebooks, or training pipelines. As the adversary moves through the environment, they may discover means of accessing additional AI-related tools, services, or applications. AI agents may also be a valuable target as they commonly have more permissions than standard user accounts on the system.

text:
Search Open Technical Databases is a technique where adversaries search for publicly available research and technical documentation to understand how and where artificial intelligence is utilized within a victim organization. By gathering this information, an attacker can identify specific targets or tailor their attacks to be more effective. 

Because organizations frequently deploy open-source model architectures trained on proprietary data, knowledge of the underlying architecture allows an adversary to craft more realistic proxy models. To find this information, adversaries may search for publications authored by employees of the target organization. These technical materials are commonly found in academic journals, conference proceedings, pre-print repositories, and technical blogs.
name: Search Open Technical Databases
description:
Adversaries may search for publicly available research and technical documentation to learn how and where AI is used within a victim organization.
The adversary can use this information to identify targets for attack, or to tailor an existing attack to make it more effective.
Organizations often use open source model architectures trained on additional proprietary data in production.
Knowledge of this underlying architecture allows the adversary to craft more realistic proxy models ([Create Proxy AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0005)).
An adversary can search these resources for publications for authors employed at the victim organization.

Research and technical materials may exist as academic papers published in [Journals and Conference Proceedings](/techniques/AML.T0000.000), or stored in [Pre-Print Repositories](/techniques/AML.T0000.001), as well as [Technical Blogs](/techniques/AML.T0000.002).

text: Journals and Conference Proceedings is a technique involving the publication of research in premier artificial intelligence venues, including both open-access and subscription-based journals and conferences. These publications often originate from commercial labs and provide detailed descriptions of specific approaches to ensure reproducibility. However, this high level of detail can be leveraged by adversaries to implement the described methods for malicious purposes.
name: Journals and Conference Proceedings
description:
Many of the publications accepted at premier artificial intelligence conferences and journals come from commercial labs.
Some journals and conferences are open access, others may require paying for access or a membership.
These publications will often describe in detail all aspects of a particular approach for reproducibility.
This information can be used by adversaries to implement the paper.

text: Pre-Print Repositories is a technique involving the use of platforms like arXiv that host the latest academic research papers before they have undergone formal peer review. These repositories often contain research notes and technical reports that are not typically found in traditional journals or conference proceedings, and they also serve as central hubs for sharing papers that have already been accepted for publication. For an adversary, searching these repositories provides a relatively up-to-date view of the specific research topics and projects being pursued by individuals within a victim organization.
name: Pre-Print Repositories
description:
Pre-Print repositories, such as arXiv, contain the latest academic research papers that haven't been peer reviewed.
They may contain research notes, or technical reports that aren't typically published in journals or conference proceedings.
Pre-print repositories also serve as a central location to share papers that have been accepted to journals.
Searching pre-print repositories  provide adversaries with a relatively up-to-date view of what researchers in the victim organization are working on.

text: Technical Blogs is a technique where an adversary searches for blog posts published by a target organization's research labs, R&D divisions, or individual employees to gather intelligence on their artificial intelligence implementations. Unlike formal journals or pre-print repositories, these blogs often provide more practical details regarding the AI systems in use, including the specific underlying technologies, frameworks, API access methods, and particular use cases. By analyzing this information, an attacker can better understand an organization's internal AI approach and use those details to tailor a more effective attack.
name: Technical Blogs
description:
Research labs at academic institutions and company R&D divisions often have blogs that highlight their use of artificial intelligence and its application to the organization's unique problems.
Individual researchers also frequently document their work in blogposts.
An adversary may search for posts made by the target victim organization or its employees.
In comparison to [Journals and Conference Proceedings](/techniques/AML.T0000.000) and [Pre-Print Repositories](/techniques/AML.T0000.001) this material will often contain more practical aspects of the AI system.
This could include underlying technologies and frameworks used, and possibly some information about the API access and use case.
This will help the adversary better understand how that organization is using AI internally and the details of their approach that could aid in tailoring an attack.

text: Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis is a technique where an adversary researches known vulnerabilities of common AI models to identify weaknesses in a specific target. This process involves reviewing academic papers to understand the particulars of successful attacks and seeking out pre-existing implementations of those exploits. By leveraging available research and existing adversarial AI attack tools, an attacker can determine the most effective way to compromise a model or develop their own custom attacks based on established vulnerabilities.
name: Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis
description:
Much like the [Search Open Technical Databases](/techniques/AML.T0000), there is often ample research available on the vulnerabilities of common AI models. Once a target has been identified, an adversary will likely try to identify any pre-existing work that has been done for this class of models.
This will include not only reading academic papers that may identify the particulars of a successful attack, but also identifying pre-existing implementations of those attacks. The adversary may obtain [Adversarial AI Attack Implementations](/techniques/AML.T0016.000) or develop their own [Adversarial AI Attacks](/techniques/AML.T0017.000) if necessary.

text:
Acquire Public AI Artifacts is a technique where adversaries search public sources—such as cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories—to identify AI artifacts. These artifacts may include the software stack used for training and deployment, training and testing data, and model configurations and parameters. Adversaries are particularly interested in artifacts associated with a specific victim organization, as these often reveal the exact tools and approaches used in a production environment.

To find these repositories, adversaries may leverage other resources linked to the victim, such as open technical databases or victim-owned websites. Once acquired, these artifacts provide critical details about the AI task and approach, which can help an adversary create a proxy AI model. If the artifacts contain components of the actual production model, they can be used to directly craft adversarial data. Depending on the source, acquiring these artifacts may require the adversary to establish accounts by providing registration details or authentication keys. Because some artifacts are hosted on victim-controlled infrastructure, the victim may be able to identify who has accessed the data.
name: Acquire Public AI Artifacts
description:
Adversaries may search public sources, including cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories, to identify AI artifacts.
These AI artifacts may include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data, model configurations and parameters.
An adversary will be particularly interested in artifacts hosted by or associated with the victim organization as they may represent what that organization uses in a production environment.
Adversaries may identify artifact repositories via other resources associated with the victim organization (e.g. [Search Victim-Owned Websites](/techniques/AML.T0003) or [Search Open Technical Databases](/techniques/AML.T0000)).
These AI artifacts often provide adversaries with details of the AI task and approach.

AI artifacts can aid in an adversary's ability to [Create Proxy AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0005).
If these artifacts include pieces of the actual model in production, they can be used to directly [Craft Adversarial Data](/techniques/AML.T0043).
Acquiring some artifacts requires registration (providing user details such email/name), AWS keys, or written requests, and may require the adversary to [Establish Accounts](/techniques/AML.T0021).

Artifacts might be hosted on victim-controlled infrastructure, providing the victim with some information on who has accessed that data.

text: Datasets is a technique where adversaries collect public datasets to support and refine their operations. By acquiring datasets that are either used by a victim organization or are representative of the organization's data, adversaries can better stage and tailor their attacks to the specific target. These datasets may be located in cloud storage or on websites owned by the victim, and in some cases, accessing them requires the adversary to first establish accounts. Ultimately, the acquisition of these datasets allows an adversary to advance their operational capabilities and increase the precision of their attacks.
name: Datasets
description:
Adversaries may collect public datasets to use in their operations.
Datasets used by the victim organization or datasets that are representative of the data used by the victim organization may be valuable to adversaries.
Datasets can be stored in cloud storage, or on victim-owned websites.
Some datasets require the adversary to [Establish Accounts](/techniques/AML.T0021) for access.

Acquired datasets help the adversary advance their operations, stage attacks,  and tailor attacks to the victim organization.

text:
Models is a technique where adversaries acquire public models to support and refine their operations. By seeking out models used by a victim organization, or representative models that mirror them, attackers can better understand the target's system. These representative models may include specific model architectures or pre-trained models that define both the architecture and the parameters derived from training datasets.

To find these assets, adversaries often search public sources for common model architecture configuration files, such as YAML or Python files, as well as standard model storage formats including ONNX, HDF5, Pickle, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. Once acquired, these models are used to tailor attacks specifically to the victim's model, significantly advancing the effectiveness of the adversary's operations.
name: Models
description:
Adversaries may acquire public models to use in their operations.
Adversaries may seek models used by the victim organization or models that are representative of those used by the victim organization.
Representative models may include model architectures, or pre-trained models which define the architecture as well as model parameters from training on a dataset.
The adversary may search public sources for common model architecture configuration file formats such as YAML or Python configuration files, and common model storage file formats such as ONNX (.onnx), HDF5 (.h5), Pickle (.pkl), PyTorch (.pth), or TensorFlow (.pb, .tflite).

Acquired models are useful in advancing the adversary's operations and are frequently used to tailor attacks to the victim model.

text:
AI Agent Configuration is a technique where adversaries acquire publicly accessible configuration files to understand an AI agent's capabilities, gain unauthorized access to tools and data sources, or identify credentials for further attacks. These files are valuable targets because they define the agent's system prompts, behavioral settings, and the specific tools it is authorized to use.

By accessing these configurations, attackers can gain insights into the agent's internal logic and harvest secrets. Targeted files typically include system prompts containing behavioral guidelines, tool configurations such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) or IDE-specific settings, and files defining the agent's skills and workflows. Additionally, adversaries may target environment and deployment configurations, such as environment variables, to control or manipulate the agent's runtime behavior.
name: AI Agent Configuration
description:
Adversaries may acquire publicly accessible AI agent configuration files to understand agent capabilities, gain unauthorized access to tools and data sources, or identify credentials for further attacks. Configuration files define what tools an agent can use, credentials for external services, system prompts, and behavioral settings, making valuable resources for adversaries targeting AI agent deployments.

Once configuration files are acquired, adversaries may perform [Discover AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0084) to gain additional insights they can use in their operation or [Credentials from AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0083) to harvest secrets.

AI agent configuration files come in multiple forms depending on the platform and agent framework. Agent configuration files adversaries may target include:
- System prompts: Files containing agent instructions, behavioral guidelines, and internal logic.
- Tool configuration: Files defining tools the agent can utilize, including Model Context Protocol (MCP) configs (e.g., `mcp.json`, `claude_desktop_config.json`), IDE-specific configs (e.g., `.claude/settings.json`, `.vscode/tasks.json`), and framework-specific settings that define external tool and data source integrations.
- Skills and workflows: Files defining agent capabilities, behaviors, or workflows. Often a combination of instructions, scripts, and resources.
- Environment and deployment configs: Files that control agent deployment and runtime behavior, often environment variables or framework-specific configs.

text:
Search Victim-Owned Websites is a technique where adversaries search websites owned by a target organization to gather information for use during the targeting process. By analyzing these sites, attackers can find technical details regarding AI-enabled products and services, as well as organizational data such as department names, physical locations, and key employee information including roles and contact details. 

These websites often reveal insights into business operations and strategic relationships, providing actionable intelligence that allows adversaries to tailor their attacks more effectively. Furthermore, information gathered from victim-owned websites can uncover additional opportunities for further reconnaissance, such as searching open technical databases or conducting open AI vulnerability analysis.
name: Search Victim-Owned Websites
description:
Adversaries may search websites owned by the victim for information that can be used during targeting.
Victim-owned websites may contain technical details about their AI-enabled products or services.
Victim-owned websites may contain a variety of details, including names of departments/divisions, physical locations, and data about key employees such as names, roles, and contact info.
These sites may also have details highlighting business operations and relationships.

Adversaries may search victim-owned websites to gather actionable information.
This information may help adversaries tailor their attacks (e.g. [Adversarial AI Attacks](/techniques/AML.T0017.000) or [Manual Modification](/techniques/AML.T0043.003)).
Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (e.g. [Search Open Technical Databases](/techniques/AML.T0000) or [Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis](/techniques/AML.T0001))

text: Search Application Repositories is a technique where adversaries search open application repositories during the targeting phase of an operation. By utilizing platforms such as the Google Play Store, the iOS App Store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store, attackers can identify specific software targets. Adversaries often craft search queries specifically designed to find applications that contain AI-enabled components, which frequently serves as a precursor to acquiring public AI artifacts.
name: Search Application Repositories
description:
Adversaries may search open application repositories during targeting.
Examples of these include Google Play, the iOS App store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store.

Adversaries may craft search queries seeking applications that contain AI-enabled components.
Frequently, the next step is to [Acquire Public AI Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0002).

text: Create Proxy AI Model is a technique where adversaries obtain or develop models to serve as proxies for a target model used by a victim organization. These proxy models are used to simulate complete access to the target model in a fully offline environment, allowing the adversary to test attacks or analyze behaviors without interacting directly with the victim's system. To achieve this, adversaries may train their own models using representative datasets, attempt to replicate the target model by querying victim inference APIs, or leverage existing pre-trained models.
name: Create Proxy AI Model
description:
Adversaries may obtain models to serve as proxies for the target model in use at the victim organization.
Proxy models are used to simulate complete access to the target model in a fully offline manner.

Adversaries may train models from representative datasets, attempt to replicate models from victim inference APIs, or use available pre-trained models.

text: Train Proxy via Gathered AI Artifacts is a technique where an adversary trains a proxy model using AI artifacts—such as data, model architectures, and pre-trained models—that are representative of a specific target model. By leveraging these gathered components, an attacker can develop sophisticated attacks that would otherwise require a higher level of access than they currently possess. Additionally, this approach allows the adversary to validate and refine pre-existing attacks in a controlled environment without needing to interact directly with the target model.
name: Train Proxy via Gathered AI Artifacts
description:
Proxy models may be trained from AI artifacts (such as data, model architectures, and pre-trained models) that are representative of the target model gathered by the adversary.
This can be used to develop attacks that require higher levels of access than the adversary has available or as a means to validate pre-existing attacks without interacting with the target model.

text: Train Proxy via Replication is a technique where adversaries replicate a private model to mimic its behavior and performance. By repeatedly querying a victim's AI model inference API, an attacker can collect a dataset of the target model's inferences. These inferences are then used as labels to train a separate offline model that acts as a proxy. Once a closely matching replicated model is created, it serves as a valuable resource for staging further attacks, such as crafting adversarial data to evade AI models or spamming AI systems with chaff data.
name: Train Proxy via Replication
description:
Adversaries may replicate a private model.
By repeatedly querying the victim's [AI Model Inference API Access](/techniques/AML.T0040), the adversary can collect the target model's inferences into a dataset.
The inferences are used as labels for training a separate model offline that will mimic the behavior and performance of the target model.

A replicated model that closely mimic's the target model is a valuable resource in staging the attack.
The adversary can use the replicated model to [Craft Adversarial Data](/techniques/AML.T0043) for various purposes (e.g. [Evade AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0015), [Spamming AI System with Chaff Data](/techniques/AML.T0046)).

text: Use Pre-Trained Model is a technique where adversaries utilize an off-the-shelf pre-trained model as a proxy for a victim model. This approach is used to aid in staging an attack by allowing the adversary to study model behaviors or refine their methods on a similar architecture before targeting the specific victim system.
name: Use Pre-Trained Model
description: Adversaries may use an off-the-shelf pre-trained model as a proxy for the victim model to aid in staging the attack.

text: Active Scanning is a technique where an adversary probes or scans a victim system to gather information for targeting. Unlike other reconnaissance methods, this approach involves direct interaction with the victim's system. Adversaries may scan for open ports on a network to identify specific services or tools in use, including AI services or AI DevOps tools such as public AI chat agents. Additionally, they may send emails to organizational service addresses and analyze the responses for indicators that an AI agent is managing the inbox. The information gathered through active scanning helps adversaries identify targets that can be further explored through other reconnaissance methods, such as searching open technical databases, analyzing AI vulnerabilities, or gathering RAG-indexed targets.
name: Active Scanning
description:
An adversary may probe or scan the victim system to gather information for targeting. This is distinct from other reconnaissance techniques that do not involve direct interaction with the victim system.

Adversaries may scan for open ports on a potential victim's network, which can indicate specific services or tools the victim is utilizing. This could include a scan for tools related to AI DevOps or AI services themselves such as public AI chat agents (ex: [Copilot Studio Hunter](https://github.com/mbrg/power-pwn/wiki/Modules:-Copilot-Studio-Hunter-%E2%80%90-Enum)). They can also send emails to organization service addresses and inspect the replies for indicators that an AI agent is managing the inbox.

Information gained from Active Scanning may yield targets that provide opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance such as [Search Open Technical Databases](/techniques/AML.T0000), [Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis](/techniques/AML.T0001), or [Gather RAG-Indexed Targets](/techniques/AML.T0064).

text: Discover AI Artifacts is a technique where adversaries search private sources to identify and gather information about AI learning artifacts present on a system. These artifacts may include model zoos, software repositories, container registries, training and testing data management systems, and the specific software stack used for the training and deployment of models. By discovering these components, an attacker can identify specific targets for exfiltration, collection, or disruption, allowing them to tailor and improve the effectiveness of their attacks.
name: Discover AI Artifacts
description:
Adversaries may search private sources to identify AI learning artifacts that exist on the system and gather information about them.
These artifacts can include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data management systems, container registries, software repositories, and model zoos.

This information can be used to identify targets for further collection, exfiltration, or disruption, and to tailor and improve attacks.

text:
Acquire Infrastructure is a technique where adversaries buy, lease, or rent various resources to support and orchestrate their operations. This infrastructure can include physical or cloud servers, domains, mobile devices, and third-party web services, as well as free resources, though the latter are often limited. In some cases, infrastructure may consist of physical components designed to degrade or disrupt AI sensors and components, such as wearables, disguises, or printed materials.

By acquiring these solutions, adversaries can effectively stage, launch, and execute their operations. Using established third-party services often helps their activity blend in with normal network traffic. Furthermore, adversaries frequently select infrastructure that is difficult to trace back to them or that can be rapidly provisioned, modified, and shut down to maintain anonymity and operational flexibility.
name: Acquire Infrastructure
description:
Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent infrastructure for use throughout their operation.
A wide variety of infrastructure exists for hosting and orchestrating adversary operations.
Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, mobile devices, and third-party web services.
Free resources may also be used, but they are typically limited.
Infrastructure can also include physical components such as countermeasures that degrade or disrupt AI components or sensors, including printed materials, wearables, or disguises.

Use of these infrastructure solutions allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.
Solutions may help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact to third-party web services.
Depending on the implementation, adversaries may use infrastructure that makes it difficult to physically tie back to them as well as utilize infrastructure that can be rapidly provisioned, modified, and shut down.

text: AI Development Workspaces is a technique where adversaries utilize specialized computing environments to develop and stage AI-based attacks. Because creating these attacks often requires significant and expensive compute power, such as multiple GPUs, attackers leverage various platforms to obtain the necessary resources. This may include the anonymous use of free services like Google Colaboratory or the deployment of temporary cloud infrastructure through providers such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. To further evade detection and maintain operational security, adversaries may distribute their activities across multiple different workspaces.
name: AI Development Workspaces
description:
Developing and staging AI attacks often requires expensive compute resources.
Adversaries may need access to one or many GPUs in order to develop an attack.
They may try to anonymously use free resources such as Google Colaboratory, or cloud resources such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud as an efficient way to stand up temporary resources to conduct operations.
Multiple workspaces may be used to avoid detection.

text: Consumer Hardware is a technique where adversaries acquire commercial off-the-shelf hardware to conduct their attacks. By owning the physical hardware, an attacker gains complete control over the environment, allowing them to manipulate the system without restriction. Additionally, these devices are often difficult for investigators to trace, providing the adversary with a higher degree of anonymity during their operations.
name: Consumer Hardware
description:
Adversaries may acquire consumer hardware to conduct their attacks.
Owning the hardware provides the adversary with complete control of the environment. These devices can be hard to trace.

text: Domains is a technique where adversaries acquire domain names to facilitate targeting operations. Domain names serve as human-readable representations of one or more IP addresses and can be obtained through purchase or free acquisition. Within the context of AI security, adversaries may specifically target expired domains that are already listed as URLs within large AI datasets. By acquiring these domains, attackers can replace legitimate data points with poisoned examples, effectively poisoning the datasets used for model training.
name: Domains
description:
Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

Adversaries may use acquired domains for a variety of purposes (see [ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/)). Large AI datasets are often distributed as a list of URLs to individual datapoints. Adversaries may acquire expired domains that are included in these datasets and replace individual datapoints with poisoned examples ([Publish Poisoned Datasets](/techniques/AML.T0019)).

text: Physical Countermeasures is a technique where adversaries acquire or manufacture physical objects to aid or support an attack. These components are used to disrupt or degrade a model's performance, such as through the use of decoys, disguises, or adversarial patterns printed on T-shirts and stickers. Additionally, these countermeasures may be employed to interfere with the sensors used for data capture, utilizing tools such as light bulbs or laser pointers to degrade the quality of the input.
name: Physical Countermeasures
description:
Adversaries may acquire or manufacture physical countermeasures to aid or support their attack.

These components may be used to disrupt or degrade the model, such as adversarial patterns printed on stickers or T-shirts, disguises, or decoys. They may also be used to disrupt or degrade the sensors used in capturing data, such as laser pointers, light bulbs, or other tools.

text:
Serverless is a technique where adversaries purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as AWS Lambda functions, Cloudflare Workers, or Google Apps Scripts, to support their targeting operations. By utilizing these environments, attackers can obscure the origin of their activities, making it more difficult for defenders to attribute the infrastructure back to the adversary.

The serverless runtime environment can be used to respond directly to infected machines or to proxy traffic to an adversary-controlled command and control server. Because the resulting traffic originates from the subdomains of reputable cloud providers, it often blends in with legitimate network activity, making it difficult to distinguish from ordinary traffic. This characteristic can be further leveraged to bypass Content Security Policies that are designed to prevent the retrieval of content from unauthorized or arbitrary locations.
name: Serverless
description:
Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting. By utilizing serverless infrastructure, adversaries can make it more difficult to attribute infrastructure used during operations back to them.

Once acquired, the serverless runtime environment can be leveraged to either respond directly to infected machines or to Proxy traffic to an adversary-owned command and control server. As traffic generated by these functions will appear to come from subdomains of common cloud providers, it may be difficult to distinguish from ordinary traffic to these providers. This can be used to bypass a Content Security Policy which prevent retrieving content from arbitrary locations.

text:
AI Service Proxies is a technique where adversaries utilize commercial proxy services that resell access to frontier model APIs and other AI services. This infrastructure allows attackers to conduct large-scale campaigns, such as performing data exfiltration via distillation, generating malicious commands for offensive cyber operations, or creating content for spearphishing through social engineering LLMs.

Because these commercial proxies distribute traffic across multiple accounts and various cloud platforms, the resulting mix of traffic makes it difficult for defenders to detect and block malicious activity. Additionally, malicious actors may employ LLM Jacking attacks to steal victim accounts, which are then resold as part of these proxy services.
name: AI Service Proxies
description:
Adversaries may utilize commercial proxy services that resell access to AI services such as frontier model APIs.

This infrastructure can be used to conduct large-scale campaigns to perform [Exfiltration via AI Inference API](/techniques/AML.T0024) via distillation. Adversaries may also use this infrastructure to [Generate Malicious Commands](/techniques/AML.T0102) for offensive cyber operations, or to generate content for [Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM](/techniques/AML.T0052.000).

Commercial AI service proxies distribute traffic from different accounts and various cloud platforms. The mix of traffic can make malicious activity difficult to detect and block [\[1\]][1].

Malicious actors conduct [LLM Jacking](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0030) attacks to gain access to victim accounts which they resell access to in their proxy services [\[2\]][2].

[1]: https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks
[2]: https://sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack/

text: AI Supply Chain Compromise is a technique where adversaries gain initial access to a system by compromising specific components of the AI supply chain. This approach involves targeting unique elements such as the underlying hardware, the training data and its associated annotations, various layers of the AI software stack, or the AI model itself. In certain scenarios, an attacker may require secondary access to fully execute their objectives after successfully compromising these supply chain components.
name: AI Supply Chain Compromise
description:
Adversaries may gain initial access to a system by compromising the unique portions of the AI supply chain.
This could include [Hardware](/techniques/AML.T0010.000), [Data](/techniques/AML.T0010.002) and its annotations, parts of the AI [AI Software](/techniques/AML.T0010.001) stack, or the [Model](/techniques/AML.T0010.003) itself.
In some instances the attacker will need secondary access to fully carry out an attack using compromised components of the supply chain.

text: Hardware is a technique where adversaries target AI systems by disrupting or manipulating the hardware supply chain. This approach focuses on the physical infrastructure required to run AI models, which often includes specialized hardware such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), or embedded devices, as well as standard Central Processing Units (CPUs) that have been optimized for AI operations.
name: Hardware
description: Adversaries may target AI systems by disrupting or manipulating the hardware supply chain. AI models often run on specialized hardware such as GPUs, TPUs, or embedded devices, but may also be optimized to operate on CPUs.

text:
AI Software is a technique where adversaries target software packages commonly used in AI-enabled systems or the AI DevOps lifecycle. This includes deep learning frameworks like PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Jax, generative AI integration frameworks such as LangChain and LangFlow, as well as inference engines and AI DevOps tools. Attackers may target the dependency chains of these packages, configuration files, or example usage distributed via Jupyter notebooks.

To execute this technique, adversaries may compromise legitimate packages or publish malicious software to namesquatted locations. They may specifically target package names that are hallucinated by large language models or perform an AI supply chain rug pull, where a legitimate package is initially published to gain a critical mass of users before being replaced with a malicious version.
name: AI Software
description:
Adversaries may target software packages that are commonly used in AI-enabled systems or are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle. This can include deep learning frameworks used to build AI models (e.g. PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax), generative AI integration frameworks (e.g. LangChain, LangFlow), inference engines, and AI DevOps tools. They may also target the dependency chains of any of these software packages [\[1\]][1]. Additionally, adversaries may target specific components used by AI software such as configuration files [\[2\]][2] or example usage of AI packages, which may be distributed in Jupyter notebooks [\[3\]][3].

Adversaries may compromise legitimate packages [\[4\]][4] or publish malicious software to a namesquatted location [\[1\]][1]. They may target package names that are hallucinated by large language models [\[5\]][5] (see: Publish Hallucinated Entities). They may also perform a [AI Supply Chain Rug Pull](/techniques/AML.T0109) in which they first publish a legitimate package and then publish a malicious version once they reach a critical mass of users.

[1]: https://pytorch.org/blog/compromised-nightly-dependency/ "Compromised PyTorch-nightly dependency chain between December 25th and December 30th, 2022."
[2]: https://www.pillar.security/blog/new-vulnerability-in-github-copilot-and-cursor-how-hackers-can-weaponize-code-agents "New Vulnerability in GitHub Copilot and Cursor: How Hackers Can Weaponize Code Agents"
[3]: https://medium.com/mlearning-ai/careful-who-you-colab-with-fa8001f933e7 "Careful Who You Colab With: abusing google colaboratory"
[4]: https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/ "Security Update for Amazon Q Developer Extension for Visual Studio Code (Version #1.84)"
[5]: https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/cybercrime-and-digital-threats/slopsquatting-when-ai-agents-hallucinate-malicious-packages "Slopsquatting: When AI Agents Hallucinate Malicious Packages"

text: Data is a technique used by adversaries as a key vector for supply chain compromise within AI projects. Because AI systems rely heavily on data, attackers may target publicly available open-source datasets or private datasets to introduce malicious content. This compromise can occur through the poisoning of training data or the inclusion of traditional malware. Additionally, adversaries may target the labeling phase of private dataset creation by infiltrating or manipulating the outside labeling services used to generate data labels, thereby poisoning the dataset.
name: Data
description:
Data is a key vector of supply chain compromise for adversaries.
Every AI project will require some form of data.
Many rely on large open source datasets that are publicly available.
An adversary could rely on compromising these sources of data.
The malicious data could be a result of [Poison Training Data](/techniques/AML.T0020) or include traditional malware.

An adversary can also target private datasets in the labeling phase.
The creation of private datasets will often require the hiring of outside labeling services.
An adversary can poison a dataset by modifying the labels being generated by the labeling service.

text: Model is a technique involving the use of AI-enabled systems that often rely on open-source models. In many cases, organizations utilize these external models as a foundation for fine-tuning, where a pre-existing model is downloaded and then refined using a smaller, private dataset. Because loading these models frequently requires the execution of saved code contained within the model file, they can be compromised through traditional malware or specialized adversarial AI techniques.
name: Model
description:
AI-enabled systems often rely on open sourced models in various ways.
Most commonly, the victim organization may be using these models for fine tuning.
These models will be downloaded from an external source and then used as the base for the model as it is tuned on a smaller, private dataset.
Loading models often requires executing some saved code in the form of a saved model file.
These can be compromised with traditional malware, or through some adversarial AI techniques.

text: Container Registry is a technique where an adversary compromises a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image to overwrite an existing container name or tag. By doing so, the adversary ensures that users and automated CI/CD pipelines pull the malicious image, thereby compromising the AI supply chain across development and deployment environments. Because container images often include AI models, this technique can be used to deliver a manipulated AI model to the target system.
name: Container Registry
description:
An adversary may compromise a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image and overwriting an existing container name and/or tag. Users of the container registry as well as automated CI/CD pipelines may pull the adversary's container image, compromising their AI Supply Chain. This can affect development and deployment environments.

Container images may include AI models, so the compromised image could have an AI model which was manipulated by the adversary (See [Manipulate AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0018)).

text:
AI Agent Tool is a technique where adversaries target the tools used by AI agents to compromise a victim's AI supply chain. These tools extend the capabilities of AI agents, enabling them to interact with external services, connect to data sources, access the internet, run system tools, and execute code. Because AI agents often possess broad permissions and access to a victim's system through these integrations, they are highly attractive targets for attackers.

Compromised or poisoned agent tools may contain malicious code or prompt injections designed to manipulate the agent's behavior or alter how other tools are invoked. This can lead to severe outcomes, such as the exfiltration of private user data. The risk is amplified by the rapid proliferation of these tools, which are frequently distributed via open-source repositories like GitHub, specialized hubs, and package registries such as NPM. Additionally, the use of remotely-hosted tools creates an environment where malicious tools can spread quickly, often bypassing necessary security safeguards.
name: AI Agent Tool
description:
Adversaries may target AI agent tools as a means to compromise a victim's AI supply chain. Tools add capabilities to AI agents, allowing them to interact with other services, connect to data sources, access internet resources, run system tools, and execute code. They are an attractive target for adversaries because compromising an AI agent can provide them with broad accesses and permissions on the victim's system via the agent's other tools.

Poisoned agent tools (See [AI Agent Tool Poisoning](/techniques/AML.T0110)) can contain malicious code or [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051)s that manipulate the agent's behavior and even modify how other tools are called. Adversaries have successfully used a poisoned MCP server to exfiltrate private user data [\[5\]][koi].

Agent tools have exploded in popularity, with thousands of MCP servers available publicly [\[2\]][glama]. They are often released on open-source software repositories such as GitHub, indexed on hubs specific to MCP servers [\[3\]][mcp-hub][\[4\]][mcp-server-hub], and published to package registries such as NPM. AI agents can also be connected to remotely-hosted tools [\[5\]][remote-mcp]. This creates an environment where malicious tools can proliferate rapidly and safeguards are often not in place.

[koi]: https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft "First Malicious MCP in the Wild: The Postmark Backdoor That's Stealing Your Emails"
[glama]: https://glama.ai/mcp/servers "Glama"
[mcp-hub]: https://www.mcphub.ai/ "MCP Hub"
[mcp-server-hub]: https://mcpserverhub.com/ "MCP Server Hub"
[remote-mcp]: https://mcpservers.org/remote-mcp-servers "Remote MCP Servers"

text: User Execution is a technique where an adversary relies on specific actions performed by a user to achieve code execution. This process often involves manipulating a user into inadvertently running unsafe code, which may be introduced through an AI supply chain compromise. Additionally, adversaries may employ social engineering tactics to trick users into executing malicious code, such as persuading them to open a malicious link or document file.
name: User Execution
description:
An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution.
Users may inadvertently execute unsafe code introduced via [AI Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010).
Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link.

text: Unsafe AI Artifacts is a technique where adversaries develop malicious AI models or components that cause deleterious effects when executed. This technique is often used to establish persistent access to targeted systems. These unsafe artifacts may be introduced into an environment through an AI supply chain compromise. A common vector for this attack is the serialization of models used for storage, transfer, and loading; if these serialized formats are loaded without proper security checks, they can provide an opportunity for unauthorized code execution.
name: Unsafe AI Artifacts
description:
Adversaries may develop unsafe AI artifacts that when executed have a deleterious effect.
The adversary can use this technique to establish persistent access to systems.
These models may be introduced via a [AI Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010).

Serialization of models is a popular technique for model storage, transfer, and loading.
However, this format without proper checking presents an opportunity for code execution.

text: Malicious Package is a technique where adversaries develop software packages that cause harmful effects when imported by a user. These packages are often designed to appear useful for AI-related tasks and may behave as expected to avoid detection. They are typically introduced into a system through an AI supply chain compromise, allowing the attacker to execute malicious code while remaining inconspicuous to the user.
name: Malicious Package
description:
Adversaries may develop malicious software packages that when imported by a user have a deleterious effect.
Malicious packages may behave as expected to the user. They may be introduced via [AI Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010). They may not present as obviously malicious to the user and may appear to be useful for an AI-related task.

text: Poisoned AI Agent Tool is a technique where a victim invokes a compromised tool while interacting with their AI agent. These poisoned tools are designed to execute malicious actions, such as performing LLM prompt injections or unauthorized AI agent tool invocations. Such tools may be introduced into a victim's environment through malicious AI software or by configuring the agent to connect to compromised remote tools.
name: Poisoned AI Agent Tool
description:
A victim may invoke a poisoned tool when interacting with their AI agent. A poisoned tool may execute an [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051) or perform [AI Agent Tool Invocation](/techniques/AML.T0053).

Poisoned AI agent tools may be introduced into the victim's environment via [AI Software](/techniques/AML.T0010.001), or the user may configure their agent to connect to remote tools.

text: Malicious Link is a technique where an adversary relies on a user clicking a harmful link to achieve code execution. This method often employs social engineering to trick users into interacting with the link, typically as a follow-on action from a spearphishing attempt. Once clicked, the link may trigger the exploitation of browser or application vulnerabilities for client execution or direct the user to download a malicious file. In the context of AI systems, adversaries can leverage malicious links to gain unauthorized access; for instance, an AI Agent that fails to validate website origin headers may accept connections from any site, allowing an attacker to bypass network restrictions and access previously unreachable resources.
name: Malicious Link
description:
An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to click on a link that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from Spearphishing Link. Clicking on a link may also lead to other execution techniques such as exploitation of a browser or application vulnerability via Exploitation for Client Execution. Links may also lead users to download files that require execution via Malicious File.

There are many ways an adversary can leverage malicious links to gain access to a victim system via an AI system. For example, an AI Agent that is configured to not validate website origin headers will accept connections from any website, allowing adversaries the ability to get around previously inaccessible network.

text: Valid Accounts is a technique where adversaries obtain and abuse the credentials of existing accounts to gain initial access to a system. These credentials may include individual usernames and passwords or API keys that provide access to various AI resources and services. By using compromised credentials, an adversary can access additional AI artifacts and perform discovery activities. Furthermore, this technique may grant the adversary increased privileges, such as write access to AI artifacts used during the development or production phases.
name: Valid Accounts
description:
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access.
Credentials may take the form of usernames and passwords of individual user accounts or API keys that provide access to various AI resources and services.

Compromised credentials may provide access to additional AI artifacts and allow the adversary to perform [Discover AI Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0007).
Compromised credentials may also grant an adversary increased privileges such as write access to AI artifacts used during development or production.

text: Discover AI Model Ontology is a technique where adversaries identify the structure and categories of an AI model's output space, such as the specific types of objects a model is capable of detecting. This discovery can be achieved through repeated queries designed to force the model to enumerate its possible outputs, or by analyzing external sources like configuration files and technical documentation. By uncovering the model ontology, an adversary gains a better understanding of how the victim is utilizing the AI, which enables them to develop more precise and targeted attacks.
name: Discover AI Model Ontology
description:
Adversaries may discover the ontology of an AI model's output space, for example, the types of objects a model can detect.
The adversary may discovery the ontology by repeated queries to the model, forcing it to enumerate its output space.
Or the ontology may be discovered in a configuration file or in documentation about the model.

The model ontology helps the adversary understand how the model is being used by the victim.
It is useful to the adversary in creating targeted attacks.

text: Discover AI Model Family is a technique where adversaries attempt to identify the general family of an AI model. This information may be gathered by reviewing available documentation or by analyzing the model's responses to carefully constructed examples to categorize it. By determining the model family, an adversary can better identify specific vulnerabilities and tailor their attacks to be more effective against that particular architecture.
name: Discover AI Model Family
description:
Adversaries may discover the general family of model.
General information about the model may be revealed in documentation, or the adversary may use carefully constructed examples and analyze the model's responses to categorize it.

Knowledge of the model family can help the adversary identify means of attacking the model and help tailor the attack.

text: Evade AI Model is a technique where adversaries manipulate data to prevent an AI model from correctly identifying content or to fool a model that expects authentic data. This is achieved by crafting adversarial data or generating deepfakes. The primary purpose of this technique is to bypass downstream tasks where AI is utilized, such as evading AI-based network scanning or virus and malware detection to facilitate traditional cyber attacks. Additionally, the use of deepfakes for AI model evasion can be used to gain initial access to systems that rely on AI-based biometric authentication.
name: Evade AI Model
description:
Adversaries can [Craft Adversarial Data](/techniques/AML.T0043) that prevents an AI model from correctly identifying the contents of the data or [Generate Deepfakes](/techniques/AML.T0088) that fools an AI model expecting authentic data.

This technique can be used to evade a downstream task where AI is utilized. The adversary may evade AI-based virus/malware detection or network scanning towards the goal of a traditional cyber attack. AI model evasion through deepfake generation may also provide initial access to systems that use AI-based biometric authentication.

text: Obtain Capabilities is a technique where adversaries search for and acquire software capabilities to support their operations. These capabilities may include specialized tools designed for adversarial AI attacks or generic software tools that are repurposed for malicious intent. In either case, the adversary may modify or customize these tools to better target a specific AI-enabled system.
name: Obtain Capabilities
description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain software capabilities for use in their operations.
Capabilities may be specific to AI-based attacks [Adversarial AI Attack Implementations](/techniques/AML.T0016.000) or generic software tools repurposed for malicious intent ([Software Tools](/techniques/AML.T0016.001)). In both instances, an adversary may modify or customize the capability to aid in targeting a particular AI-enabled system.

text: Adversarial AI Attack Implementations is a technique where adversaries seek out and utilize existing open-source implementations of AI attacks to target systems. Because the research community frequently publishes code to ensure reproducibility and advance study, specialized libraries designed for research—such as CleverHans, the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and FoolBox—can be weaponized for malicious purposes. Additionally, adversaries may repurpose tools that were not originally intended for adversarial AI attacks to facilitate their operations.
name: Adversarial AI Attack Implementations
description: Adversaries may search for existing open source implementations of AI attacks. The research community often publishes their code for reproducibility and to further future research. Libraries intended for research purposes, such as CleverHans, the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and FoolBox, can be weaponized by an adversary. Adversaries may also obtain and use tools that were not originally designed for adversarial AI attacks as part of their attack.

text: Software Tools is a technique where adversaries search for and obtain software to support their operations. This process often involves repurposing software designed for legitimate use for malicious intent, or modifying and customizing existing tools to achieve specific objectives. Notably, the software tools used to support attacks on AI systems are not necessarily AI-based themselves.
name: Software Tools
description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain software tools to support their operations.
Software designed for legitimate use may be repurposed by an adversary for malicious intent.
An adversary may modify or customize software tools to achieve their purpose.
Software tools used to support attacks on AI systems are not necessarily AI-based themselves.

text:
Generative AI is a technique that adversaries use to obtain and leverage artificial intelligence models, such as large language models, to assist in various stages of a cyber operation. These tools are used for malicious purposes including the generation of malware, deepfakes, malicious commands, and phishing content, as well as crafting content for retrieval.

Adversaries may acquire these capabilities by serving open-source models locally using frameworks like Ollama or vLLM, hosting them on cloud infrastructure, or utilizing AI service providers such as HuggingFace. To bypass safety restrictions and content filters, attackers may employ jailbreaking techniques or seek out "uncensored" models. These uncensored variants are either designed without guardrails, fine-tuned to remove alignment, or specifically developed and advertised for malicious use. While some of these models are built for offensive and defensive cybersecurity research, they are frequently abused by cybercriminals to execute attacks without the limitations imposed by standard AI developers.
name: Generative AI
description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain generative AI models or tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to assist them in various steps of their operation. Generative AI can be used in a variety of malicious ways, such as to generating malware, to [Generate Deepfakes](/techniques/AML.T0088), to [Generate Malicious Commands](/techniques/AML.T0102), for [Retrieval Content Crafting](/techniques/AML.T0066), or to generate [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052) content.

Adversaries may obtain open source models and serve them locally using frameworks such as [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) or [vLLM]( https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/). They may host them using cloud infrastructure. Or, they may leverage AI service providers such as HuggingFace.

They may need to jailbreak the model (see [LLM Jailbreak](/techniques/AML.T0054)) to bypass any restrictions put in place to limit the types of responses it can generate. They may also need to break the terms of service of the model's developer.

Generative AI models may also be "uncensored" meaning they are designed to generate content without any restrictions such as guardrails or content filters. Uncensored GenAI is ripe for abuse by cybercriminals [\[1\]][1] [\[2\]][2]. Models may be fine-tuned to remove alignment and guardrails [\[3\]][3] or be subjected to targeted manipulations to bypass refusal [\[4\]][4] resulting in uncensored variants of the model. Uncensored models may be built for offensive and defensive cybersecurity [\[5\]][5], which can be abused by an adversary. There are also models that are expressly designed and advertised for malicious use [\[6\]][6].

[1]: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/cybercriminal-abuse-of-large-language-models/
[2]: https://gbhackers.com/cybercriminals-exploit-llm-models/
[3]: https://erichartford.com/uncensored-models
[4]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717/
[5]: https://taico.ca/posts/whiterabbitneo/
[6]: https://gbhackers.com/wormgpt-enhanced-with-grok-and-mixtral/

text: Develop Capabilities is a technique where adversaries create their own tools and resources to support their operations. This process involves identifying specific requirements, building technical solutions, and deploying those capabilities to achieve their goals. Capabilities designed to attack AI-enabled systems are not required to be AI-based themselves; for instance, an adversary might set up websites containing adversarial information or develop Jupyter notebooks featuring obfuscated code for data exfiltration.
name: Develop Capabilities
description: Adversaries may develop their own capabilities to support operations. This process encompasses identifying requirements, building solutions, and deploying capabilities. Capabilities used to support attacks on AI-enabled systems are not necessarily AI-based themselves. Examples include setting up websites with adversarial information or creating Jupyter notebooks with obfuscated exfiltration code.

text: Adversarial AI Attacks is a technique where adversaries develop specialized methods to manipulate or deceive artificial intelligence models. These attacks can be created by leveraging existing software libraries as a foundation, implementing concepts detailed in public research papers, or developing custom-made attacks specifically tailored to a victim model's architecture and vulnerabilities.
name: Adversarial AI Attacks
description:
Adversaries may develop their own adversarial attacks.
They may leverage existing libraries as a starting point ([Adversarial AI Attack Implementations](/techniques/AML.T0016.000)).
They may implement ideas described in public research papers or develop custom made attacks for the victim model.

text: Manipulate AI Model is a technique where adversaries directly alter an AI model to change its behavior or introduce malicious code. By manipulating the model, an attacker can achieve a persistent change within the system. This process may involve poisoning the model by changing its weights, modifying the model architecture to alter its functional behavior, or embedding malware that is executed when the model is loaded.
name: Manipulate AI Model
